title: Design a scalable admin dashboard
clarifyingQuestions: Who are the users — internal ops staff, external customers, or both — and how many concurrent users do we expect?
What data domains does the dashboard cover (users, billing, content moderation, analytics) and how many distinct modules/pages?
Do we need real-time updates (e.g., live metrics) or is periodic refresh/polling acceptable?
What are the row-level permission requirements — can different admins see different subsets of data?
Is this a single product or a platform other internal teams will extend with their own modules?
What is the expected data volume per table/view (hundreds of rows vs. hundreds of thousands)?
functionalRequirements: Authenticated admins can view and search across core entities (users, orders, content) with filters and pagination
Admins can perform CRUD actions on entities subject to their role permissions
Dashboard shows summary metrics/widgets (charts, KPI tiles) on a landing page
Support bulk actions (e.g., bulk approve, bulk export) on selected rows
Audit trail of who changed what and when is viewable
Global search and per-module filtering/sorting
nonFunctionalRequirements: Initial load under ~2s on a typical corporate network; route-level code splitting to avoid shipping unused modules
Scale to tables with 100k+ rows via server-side pagination/virtualization, not client-side loading of everything
Strict RBAC enforced server-side; frontend only hides/disables UI as a UX convenience
Accessible to keyboard-only and screen-reader users (WCAG 2.1 AA) since internal tools are still subject to accessibility requirements
Resilient to partial API failures — one broken widget should not crash the whole dashboard
Auditable and observable — every admin mutation should be traceable in logs/monitoring
routeStructure:
/login
/dashboard                 (overview widgets/KPIs)
/dashboard/users           (list, filters)
/dashboard/users/:id       (detail/edit)
/dashboard/orders          (list)
/dashboard/orders/:id
/dashboard/content         (moderation queue)
/dashboard/settings
/dashboard/audit-log
/403 and /404 fallback routes

Each top-level module is its own route-level chunk (lazy loaded) so an admin who only uses "orders" never downloads the "content moderation" bundle.
componentArchitecture:
Layout shell: AppShell (nav sidebar + topbar + outlet) wraps all authenticated routes.
Per-module: ModuleListPage (table + filters + pagination) and ModuleDetailPage (form/detail view) are the two recurring templates — build one generic DataTable and one generic EntityForm and configure them per module instead of writing bespoke tables for each entity.
Shared primitives: DataTable (virtualized, sortable, server-paginated), FilterBar, Modal, ConfirmDialog, Toast, KPI Card, Chart wrapper.
Container/presentational split: "smart" page components own data-fetching (via hooks) and pass plain data + callbacks down to "dumb" presentational components, which stay easy to test and reuse.
Feature-folder structure (features/users, features/orders) keeps each module's components, hooks, and API calls colocated rather than splitting by technical layer across the whole app.
stateOwnership:
Server state (users, orders, content lists, detail records) is owned by a data-fetching library (e.g., React Query/TanStack Query or SWR) — it handles caching, refetch-on-focus, and invalidation after mutations. This is NOT duplicated into global client state.
Global client/UI state is limited to: current user/session, active role/permissions, and app-wide UI (sidebar collapsed, theme). This can live in lightweight context or a small store — Redux is unnecessary here unless there's deeply cross-cutting client state with complex update logic.
Local/ephemeral state (filter draft values, modal open/closed, selected table rows, form field state) stays in local component state or the URL (query params) so filters are shareable/bookmarkable and don't pollute global state.
apiLayer:
A thin service layer (e.g., /api/users.ts, /api/orders.ts) wraps REST (or GraphQL) calls, so components never call fetch directly. This layer normalizes response shapes and errors into a consistent { data, error } or throws a typed AppError.
React Query/SWR sits on top for caching, deduplication of in-flight requests, background revalidation, and optimistic updates on mutations (e.g., bulk approve updates the cache immediately, rolls back on failure).
For cross-module aggregation (e.g., a KPI widget needing counts from three services), consider a lightweight BFF/aggregation endpoint rather than fan-out calls from the client, to reduce waterfalls and keep the client simple.
authentication:
Session via httpOnly, secure, SameSite cookies (avoid storing tokens in localStorage to reduce XSS token-theft risk). Login flow redirects to SSO/OAuth if the org uses one.
RBAC: the user's role/permissions are fetched once at session start and used to conditionally render nav items, buttons, and routes (route guards redirect unauthorized users). This is purely a UX layer — the backend/API MUST independently verify permissions on every request, since a determined user can bypass frontend checks via direct API calls.
Sensitive actions (delete, bulk mutate) require re-confirmation and are double-checked server-side.
errorHandling:
A top-level React ErrorBoundary catches render-time crashes and shows a recoverable fallback rather than a blank white screen; module-level boundaries around each dashboard widget so one bad widget (e.g., a chart with malformed data) doesn't take down the whole page.
API errors are normalized in the service layer into typed errors (NetworkError, ValidationError, PermissionError, ServerError) and handled uniformly: validation errors surface inline on forms, permission errors show a clear "not authorized" message, network/server errors show retry affordances.
Mutations show optimistic UI where safe, with rollback and a toast on failure; destructive actions confirm before executing.
caching:
React Query/SWR provides in-memory client caching with configurable staleTime/cacheTime per query (e.g., user list cached 30s, static reference data like "roles" cached much longer).
HTTP caching headers (ETag/Last-Modified, Cache-Control) on read-heavy, slowly-changing endpoints (e.g., role definitions) so the browser/CDN can avoid refetching unchanged data.
Static assets (JS/CSS bundles) are hashed and served from a CDN with long-lived immutable cache headers; HTML is served with no-cache so new deploys are picked up immediately.
After mutations, targeted cache invalidation (not full app reload) refreshes only the affected queries.
performance:
Route-based code splitting per module (users/orders/content) so admins download only what they use; further split heavy libraries (charting) behind dynamic import.
Virtualized tables (e.g., react-window/virtualized) for large lists so only visible rows render in the DOM.
Server-side pagination, sorting, and filtering (never load 100k rows client-side and filter in JS).
Debounce search/filter inputs to avoid firing a request per keystroke; memoize expensive derived computations (useMemo) and avoid unnecessary re-renders in table rows (React.memo on row components).
Prefetch likely-next data (e.g., prefetch detail record on row hover) to make navigation feel instant.
accessibility:
Data tables use proper semantic markup (or ARIA grid roles) with row/column headers announced correctly to screen readers; sortable column headers expose aria-sort.
All interactive controls (filters, bulk-action buttons, modals) are keyboard-operable with visible focus states; modals trap focus and restore it to the triggering element on close.
Color is never the sole indicator of status (e.g., pair a red "flagged" badge with an icon/text label) to support color-blind users.
Form validation errors are announced via aria-live regions, and charts/KPIs have text alternatives (e.g., a data table view) for screen-reader users.
security:
Sanitize/escape any user-generated content rendered in the dashboard (e.g., user bios, content titles) to prevent stored XSS; rely on the framework's default escaping and avoid dangerouslySetInnerHTML unless content is sanitized server-side.
CSRF protection via SameSite cookies plus a CSRF token on state-changing requests if cookies are used for auth.
No API keys or secrets (analytics write keys, third-party service secrets) are ever embedded in frontend bundles — all privileged calls go through the backend.
All authorization decisions are re-validated server-side; the frontend RBAC is UX-only, never a security boundary.
testing:
Unit tests for the service layer (API normalization, error mapping) and pure utility functions (formatters, permission-check helpers).
Component/integration tests (Testing Library) for the DataTable (sorting, pagination, empty/error states) and forms (validation, submit success/failure), since these are reused everywhere and bugs there are high-impact.
E2E tests (Playwright/Cypress) for the critical admin workflows: login, view a list, edit a record, bulk action, and a permission-denied path — these catch integration regressions across routing, auth, and API.
Visual regression tests on the shared component library (table, cards) to catch unintended UI breaks.
deployment:
Static frontend build deployed to a CDN/edge host (Vercel/Netlify/S3+CloudFront) with immutable, hashed asset filenames; HTML entry point served without long caching so deploys propagate immediately.
Separate environments (dev/staging/prod) with environment-specific API base URLs injected at build time via env vars (never secrets, only public config).
CI pipeline: lint, typecheck, unit/integration tests, build, then automated E2E smoke tests against a preview deployment before promoting to prod; feature flags allow gradual rollout of risky new modules.
monitoring:
Error tracking (e.g., Sentry) captures unhandled exceptions and ErrorBoundary catches, tagged with route/module and user role (not PII) for triage.
Real User Monitoring/performance monitoring (Core Web Vitals, route load times) to catch regressions in slow modules like large tables.
Structured client-side logging of key admin actions (non-sensitive) feeding into product analytics to understand which modules are used and where users get stuck.
Alerting on spikes in client error rate or API error rate surfaced from the frontend, correlated with backend dashboards.
tradeoffs:
Start simple: a single global store (or even just React Query + context) is enough for most admin dashboards — do not reach for Redux/MobX until you have complex, deeply cross-cutting client state with non-trivial update logic that context/hooks genuinely struggle with; most "we need Redux" dashboards actually just need better server-state caching, which React Query already provides.
Build one generic, configurable DataTable/EntityForm rather than one bespoke component per module — the reuse pays off after the second or third module, and avoids an early over-abstracted "table framework" nobody needed yet.
GraphQL vs REST: GraphQL is attractive for a dashboard aggregating many entities, but introduces schema/tooling overhead; if there are only a handful of REST endpoints and no serious over/under-fetching problem, plain REST + a service layer is simpler to reason about and ship faster — add GraphQL or a BFF only once fan-out calls or payload mismatches become a measurable pain point.
Microfrontends are almost never justified for a single admin dashboard team — reach for that only when genuinely independent teams need independent deploy cadences for different modules; otherwise it adds massive build/runtime complexity for no benefit.

followUpQuestions: How would you handle a widget on the dashboard whose data source is down while the rest of the page works fine?
How would you design permissions so that a "read-only auditor" role sees the same pages but cannot mutate anything?
If one module's table needs to show 500k rows, what changes in your approach?
How do you prevent a slow third-party analytics script from blocking the dashboard's main thread?
How would you migrate this dashboard from one big SPA to allowing another team to ship their own module independently, if that became a real need?
spokenAnswer:
Start by restating the scope: an internal admin dashboard with multiple entity modules, RBAC, and a mix of read-heavy tables and CRUD forms. Clarify scale (rows per table, concurrent admins) and whether real-time is needed, since that changes the caching/state answer.
Then walk through structure: an AppShell with lazy-loaded module routes, built from two reusable templates — a virtualized, server-paginated DataTable and a generic EntityForm — rather than bespoke components per module.
Cover state next: server state lives in React Query (caching, invalidation, optimistic updates), global client state is minimal (session, role, theme), and ephemeral UI state stays local or in the URL. Explicitly say you're avoiding Redux/GraphQL/microfrontends unless a concrete driver (deeply cross-cutting state, real aggregation pain, independent team deploy cadence) shows up — starting simple and adding complexity only when justified is a deliberate choice, not an oversight.
Then hit auth (RBAC is UX-only, backend enforces), error handling (boundaries per widget), performance (virtualization, code splitting, debounced search), and accessibility (keyboard/table semantics).
Finish with deployment/monitoring: CDN-hosted static build, CI with E2E smoke tests, Sentry + RUM for observability, and close with the key trade-off you made (e.g., REST+service-layer over GraphQL) and why, showing you can defend a pragmatic choice under scale pressure.

title: Design a multi-role SaaS frontend (e.g., a coaching/marketplace platform with distinct coach/learner/admin roles)
clarifyingQuestions: How many distinct roles are there, and can a single user hold multiple roles simultaneously (e.g., a coach who is also a learner)?
Do roles share significant UI (e.g., messaging, profile) or are their experiences almost entirely separate?
Is this a single deployed app with role-based views, or should coach/learner/admin be separate apps/subdomains?
What is the onboarding flow — do users pick a role at signup, or is role assigned by an admin/approval process?
Are there marketplace-specific needs like search/discovery, bookings, payments, or reviews?
What devices matter most — is this primarily mobile web, desktop, or both equally?
functionalRequirements: Users can sign up/log in and land on a role-appropriate home experience
Learners can browse/search coaches, view profiles, and book sessions
Coaches can manage their availability, profile, and view/manage bookings
Admins can moderate users/listings, view platform-wide metrics, and manage disputes
Shared features across roles: messaging/notifications, profile/settings, and reviews/ratings
Support switching between roles for dual-role users without a full logout/login
nonFunctionalRequirements: Role-specific bundles are code-split so a learner never downloads the coach-management or admin bundle
Consistent design language across roles via a shared component library to keep the product coherent
Secure separation of role capabilities enforced server-side, not just via frontend routing
Responsive across mobile and desktop since marketplace browsing is often mobile-first
Accessible booking and search flows (critical conversion paths)
Resilient to partial outages (e.g., messaging down shouldn't block booking)
routeStructure:
/                          (marketing/landing, role-agnostic)
/login, /signup
/onboarding/select-role

/app                       (authenticated shell; redirects by active role)
/app/learner/discover       (search/browse coaches)
/app/learner/coach/:id
/app/learner/bookings
/app/coach/dashboard
/app/coach/availability
/app/coach/bookings
/app/admin/users
/app/admin/listings
/app/admin/reports

/app/messages              (shared across roles)
/app/settings              (shared, role-aware sections)

Role-specific route groups are separate lazy-loaded chunks; a role switcher changes the active role in session state and redirects into that role's home without a full re-auth.
componentArchitecture:
A shared AppShell (nav, role switcher, notifications bell) wraps all authenticated routes; nav items are derived from the current role's permission/config, not hardcoded per role.
Feature modules are organized per role (features/learner, features/coach, features/admin) plus a shared/ module (Profile, Messaging, Reviews, Booking widgets) used by more than one role.
Common UI primitives (buttons, cards, forms, tables) live in a shared design-system package so learner/coach/admin surfaces feel like one product, not three.
Role-specific "smart" page components fetch role-scoped data via hooks; shared components like a Booking widget accept role as a prop/config to adjust which actions are available, rather than being duplicated per role.
stateOwnership:
Server state (coach listings, bookings, messages, admin reports) is owned by a query/cache library, scoped by role-aware query keys (e.g., ['bookings', role, userId]) so switching roles doesn't leak cached data across contexts.
Global state: current user, active role (for dual-role users), and permissions — kept in a small auth/session context, not duplicated per feature.
UI state (search filters, selected date in availability calendar, open modals) stays local to the relevant feature module.
Avoid a single monolithic global store spanning all three roles' data — that couples unrelated features and makes role-based code splitting harder; scope stores per feature module instead.
apiLayer:
Service layer organized per domain (bookings.ts, listings.ts, messaging.ts, admin.ts) rather than per role, since some domains (bookings) are read/written by multiple roles with different permissions — the backend enforces who can do what.
A BFF or lightweight aggregation endpoint can simplify the learner "discover" page (needs coach info + availability + ratings in one call) to avoid client-side waterfalls, especially important for a mobile-first browsing experience.
Mutations (booking a session, approving a listing) go through the service layer with consistent error typing and optimistic updates where UX benefits (e.g., instantly showing "booked" while confirming server-side).
authentication:
Single sign-on session (httpOnly cookie) across all roles; the JWT/session payload includes the user's role(s) and permissions, refreshed on role switch or periodically.
Route guards check the active role client-side to redirect users to the right home and hide irrelevant nav — again, purely UX; the backend must independently authorize every request based on the authenticated user's actual roles/permissions, since a learner could otherwise attempt to call coach or admin APIs directly.
Admin routes get extra scrutiny: consider requiring step-up auth (re-auth or MFA) for sensitive admin actions like account bans or payout overrides.
errorHandling:
Error boundaries scoped per role-module so a crash in the admin reports page doesn't affect the learner discovery flow (relevant for dual-role users switching contexts).
Booking flow (revenue-critical) gets explicit, user-friendly error states at each step (search fails, slot no longer available, payment declines) rather than a generic error toast — marketplace conversion is sensitive to friction here.
Centralized error-to-message mapping so the same backend error code renders consistent, role-appropriate copy across learner/coach/admin surfaces.
caching:
Query caching per role-scoped keys with short staleTime for volatile data (availability, booking status) and longer staleTime for stable data (coach profile, reviews).
CDN caching for public marketing pages and coach public profile pages (which can be statically generated or ISR'd if using a framework like Next.js) since these are read-heavy and SEO-relevant.
HTTP cache headers for search/discover results are short-lived (or bypassed) given availability changes frequently; invalidate booking-related caches immediately after a successful booking mutation.
performance:
Code-split by role so each role's bundle stays small; further split rarely-used admin sub-tools behind their own chunks.
Virtualize long lists (coach search results, admin user tables) and paginate server-side.
Lazy-load below-the-fold marketplace content (reviews, related coaches) and use image optimization/responsive images for coach profile photos, a major payload contributor.
Debounce search-as-you-type and cancel in-flight stale search requests to keep discovery feeling responsive.
accessibility:
Search/filter controls on the discovery page are fully keyboard-operable with clear labels (not just icon buttons) and announce result counts via aria-live so screen-reader users get feedback after filtering.
Booking calendar/availability picker uses accessible date-picker patterns (arrow-key navigation, announced selected date) since this is a core conversion flow.
Role switcher and nav are reachable via keyboard with visible focus, and role-specific icons/badges pair color with text/icon so status isn't conveyed by color alone.
security:
Strict server-side authorization per role for every endpoint (a learner token must never be able to fetch another coach's private earnings data, for example) — frontend role-based rendering is UX only.
Sanitize any user-generated content shown across roles (coach bios, learner reviews, admin dispute notes) to prevent stored XSS.
Payment/booking flows never handle raw card data or secret keys in the frontend — use a payment provider's client-side tokenization SDK and keep secret keys server-side only (see the payment/checkout design for detail).
Rate-limit and validate messaging inputs to prevent spam/abuse between learner and coach.
testing:
Unit tests for role-permission derivation logic (given a user's roles, what nav/actions should be visible) since bugs here cause visible UX/security confusion.
Integration tests per role's critical flow: learner search-to-booking, coach availability management, admin listing moderation.
E2E tests covering role switching for dual-role accounts and the full booking happy path plus at least one failure path (slot taken, payment declined).
Contract/API tests ensuring the frontend's assumptions about response shapes match backend reality, especially for the aggregated discover endpoint.
deployment:
Single SPA (or Next.js app) deployed to CDN/edge, with role-based route chunks lazy-loaded — no need for separate deployable apps per role unless team structure demands it.
Staging environment mirrors production role configurations for QA across all three roles; feature flags gate new marketplace features (e.g., a new booking flow) for gradual rollout to a subset of coaches/learners.
CI runs role-specific test suites in parallel and blocks deploy on failures in any role's critical path.
monitoring:
Error tracking tagged by role and route so spikes in, say, coach-availability errors are triaged separately from learner-search errors.
Funnel analytics on the booking flow (search → view profile → select slot → confirm → pay) to spot drop-off, plus Core Web Vitals tracked per role since learner-facing discovery is most performance/conversion sensitive.
Business-relevant client logging (bookings started/completed, listings created) feeding product analytics, kept separate from technical error logs.
tradeoffs:
Start with one app with role-based route groups rather than three separate apps/microfrontends per role — splitting into independent deployables only pays off once distinct teams own each role's surface and need independent release cycles; before that, it's pure overhead (duplicated tooling, shared-component syncing pain).
Prefer plain REST/service-layer calls per domain over GraphQL unless the discover page's aggregation needs (coach + availability + reviews in one view) become a real, measurable over-fetching/waterfall problem — then a small BFF endpoint is a lighter first step than adopting a full GraphQL layer.
Keep global state minimal (auth/role context) rather than centralizing all cross-role data in one big store; that avoids coupling and keeps the role-based code splitting effective. Only introduce a heavier state manager if you find yourself prop-drilling the same complex, frequently-updated state across many disconnected component trees.
Dual-role support (switch without logout) adds real complexity (query-key scoping, nav rebuilding) — if the product only rarely has dual-role users, it may be simpler to require a logout/login role switch initially and revisit if usage data shows it's a common, painful pattern.

followUpQuestions: How would you support a user who is both a coach and a learner switching context without losing their place?
How do you prevent a learner from seeing coach-only data if they tamper with the frontend role state?
How would you design the discover/search page to stay fast as the number of coaches grows into the tens of thousands?
What would change if messaging needed to be real-time (WebSocket-based) instead of polling?
How would you decide when it's time to split this into separate deployable apps per role?
spokenAnswer:
Open by clarifying roles, whether dual-role exists, and whether this is one app or several — that answer drives everything downstream.
Describe the route structure: a shared authenticated shell with role-based lazy-loaded route groups, plus shared modules (messaging, profile, reviews) used across roles so the product feels cohesive, not siloed.
Cover component architecture and a shared design-system package so learner/coach/admin UI stays visually consistent, then explain state ownership: server state cached per role-scoped keys, minimal global auth/role context, local UI state per feature — explicitly noting you're avoiding one giant cross-role store or premature GraphQL/microfrontend adoption until there's a concrete driver like independent team ownership or real over-fetching pain.
Walk through the booking flow as the revenue-critical path: API layer with optional BFF aggregation for discovery, careful error handling at each booking step, and backend-enforced authorization since frontend role checks are UX only.
Close with performance (code-splitting per role, virtualized search results), accessibility on the booking calendar, and monitoring focused on the booking funnel — then name your key trade-off (single app with route groups vs. separate apps) and the concrete signal that would make you revisit it.

title: Design an e-commerce/marketplace frontend
clarifyingQuestions: Is this B2C retail, a multi-vendor marketplace, or both — does it need seller-facing tooling too?
What is the expected catalog size (hundreds vs. millions of SKUs) and how is search/discovery expected to work (facets, full-text, recommendations)?
Is SEO important for product/category pages (implying SSR/SSG), or is this primarily an app-like experience behind login?
What payment providers and regions are supported, and are there compliance requirements (PCI DSS)?
Do we need guest checkout, and how important is mobile web performance/conversion?
Is inventory/pricing real-time sensitive (flash sales, limited stock) requiring live updates?
functionalRequirements: Users can browse categories, search products, and filter/sort results
Users can view product detail pages with images, variants (size/color), price, and stock status
Users can add to cart, view/edit cart, and complete checkout (address, shipping, payment)
Users can view order history and order status
Guest checkout and authenticated checkout are both supported
Sellers (if marketplace) can manage listings and view orders for their products
nonFunctionalRequirements: Fast Time-to-Interactive and good Core Web Vitals on product and category pages — directly tied to conversion and SEO ranking
SEO-friendly rendering (SSR/SSG) for public catalog pages
Checkout flow must be highly reliable and resilient to partial failures (never lose cart state)
PCI compliance — no raw card data touches the frontend's own code/servers
Accessible browsing and checkout flows (legal requirement in many regions for retail)
Scales to traffic spikes (flash sales, holiday traffic) without degrading
routeStructure:
/                          (home, SSR/SSG)
/category/:slug           (category listing, SSR/SSG + client filters)
/product/:slug            (PDP, SSR/SSG for SEO)
/cart
/checkout/address
/checkout/shipping
/checkout/payment
/checkout/confirmation
/account/orders
/account/orders/:id
/account/settings
/seller/dashboard          (if marketplace; separate lazy chunk)
/seller/listings

Catalog/PDP routes favor server rendering (SSR/SSG via a framework like Next.js) for SEO and fast first paint; checkout and account routes can be client-rendered SPA-style behind auth since SEO doesn't matter there.
componentArchitecture:
Catalog module: ProductGrid, ProductCard, FilterSidebar, SortDropdown — built to be server-rendered with client-side hydration for interactivity (filters update via URL params so results are shareable/cacheable).
PDP module: image gallery, variant selector, price/stock display, add-to-cart button, reviews section (can lazy-load below the fold).
Cart/checkout module: a multi-step checkout is broken into small, independently testable steps (AddressForm, ShippingOptions, PaymentStep, OrderSummary) coordinated by a checkout flow controller that persists progress.
Cross-cutting: a persistent CartWidget in the header reflects cart state everywhere; a shared design-system package (buttons, price display, badges) keeps catalog/checkout/account visually consistent.
stateOwnership:
Server state (product data, cart contents when the user is logged in, order history) is fetched/cached via a query library, with the cart specifically also mirrored server-side so it survives across devices/sessions for logged-in users.
Cart state for guests can live in local/session storage as a fallback but should sync to a server-side cart as soon as the user's session allows, to avoid divergent client/server sources of truth.
Global client state is minimal: auth status, currency/locale, and cart summary count (for the header badge) — kept in a small context, not a heavyweight global store.
Checkout step state (which step you're on, in-progress form values) is local to the checkout flow, persisted to sessionStorage so a refresh doesn't lose progress, but cleared/rehydrated from server truth on step transitions.
apiLayer:
Service layer per domain: catalog.ts (search/browse/PDP), cart.ts, checkout.ts, orders.ts. Catalog reads can be heavily cached/CDN-served; cart/checkout writes are not cached and go through careful error handling.
For SSR pages (category, PDP), data is fetched server-side at request/build time to enable fast first paint and SEO; client-side hydration then takes over for filters/interactions using the same service layer.
Checkout API calls are idempotent where possible (e.g., idempotency keys on "place order") to safely handle retries after network blips without double-charging or double-creating orders.
authentication:
Session via httpOnly cookies; guest checkout works without an account by using a guest/session-scoped cart and order lookup via order ID + email rather than requiring login.
Account pages and seller dashboard require authentication with route guards redirecting to login; as always, the backend independently verifies that a user can only view/modify their own orders/listings — frontend checks are UX convenience only.
Step-up verification (e.g., re-enter CVV or 3D Secure) is handled by the payment provider's flow, not built custom.
errorHandling:
Checkout is the highest-stakes flow: each step validates input inline, and payment failures show specific, actionable messages (card declined vs. network error vs. out-of-stock-at-payment-time) rather than a generic "something went wrong."
Cart/inventory races (item goes out of stock between add-to-cart and checkout) are handled explicitly — recheck stock at the payment step and surface a clear message with an easy path to adjust the cart.
Error boundaries around non-critical widgets (recommendations, reviews) so their failure never blocks browsing or checkout.
All network errors on checkout preserve the user's entered data (never clear a filled form on error).
caching:
Category/PDP pages use SSR/SSG with CDN caching (e.g., stale-while-revalidate) since product content changes infrequently relative to traffic; cache is invalidated/revalidated on price or stock changes via webhook-triggered rebuilds or short TTLs.
Search/filter results may be cached briefly client-side (query library) but avoided for highly volatile inventory (flash sales) where freshness matters more than cache hits.
Static assets (images, JS/CSS) served from CDN with long-lived immutable caching; product images use responsive/optimized formats (WebP/AVIF) with CDN-based resizing.
Cart and checkout data are never cached at the HTTP layer (Cache-Control: no-store) since they're user- and time-sensitive.
performance:
SSR/SSG for catalog pages to optimize LCP and SEO; hydrate progressively so interactive elements (add-to-cart) become usable quickly even before the whole page hydrates.
Image optimization (responsive srcset, lazy loading below the fold, priority loading for the hero/first product image) since images dominate PDP payload.
Code-split checkout and account/seller modules away from the public catalog bundle; defer non-critical scripts (reviews widgets, chat widgets, analytics) until after main content is interactive.
Virtualize long category listing pages or use classic pagination/infinite scroll with windowing for very large result sets.
accessibility:
Product cards and filters are keyboard-navigable with clear focus states; filter changes announce result counts via aria-live.
Checkout forms have properly associated labels, inline error messages linked via aria-describedby, and logical tab order across multi-step flow; a persistent order summary is available to screen-reader users at each step.
Color is never the sole signal for stock status (e.g., "Only 2 left" text plus color) and images have meaningful alt text (product name/variant) rather than generic "product image."
security:
PCI compliance: card data is never handled directly by the frontend's own code — a payment provider's hosted fields or client-side SDK (e.g., Stripe Elements) tokenizes card details, and the token (not the card number) is sent to the backend; no secret/API keys for the payment provider are ever embedded in frontend bundles.
Sanitize any user-generated content (reviews, seller descriptions) to prevent stored XSS.
CSRF protection on cart/checkout mutations if using cookie-based sessions; rate-limit login/checkout endpoints to mitigate credential-stuffing and carding attacks (enforced server-side).
All pricing/discount logic is validated server-side — never trust a client-sent price or discount code application.
testing:
Unit tests for cart math (subtotal, tax, discount application) since pricing bugs are costly and easy to get subtly wrong.
Integration tests for the checkout step components (validation, moving between steps, error states).
E2E tests covering the full purchase happy path (browse → add to cart → checkout → confirmation) plus key failure paths (declined payment, out-of-stock at checkout, guest vs. logged-in checkout).
Visual regression tests on PDP and cart components, and performance budget tests (Lighthouse CI) on catalog pages to catch regressions in Core Web Vitals before they hit production.
deployment:
Hybrid rendering deployment (e.g., Next.js on Vercel or similar) supporting SSR/SSG for catalog and static hosting/CDN for assets; incremental static regeneration or webhook-triggered rebuilds keep catalog pages fresh without full redeploys.
Blue/green or canary deploys for checkout changes given how business-critical that flow is; feature flags allow testing a new checkout flow with a small percentage of traffic before full rollout.
Separate staging environment with sandbox payment provider credentials for full checkout testing without real charges.
monitoring:
Real User Monitoring on Core Web Vitals specifically for catalog/PDP pages, since these directly affect conversion and SEO ranking.
Funnel analytics across the full purchase funnel (view PDP → add to cart → begin checkout → complete purchase) with drop-off tracked per step to catch regressions or friction.
Error tracking with special alerting sensitivity on checkout/payment errors (low tolerance, page finance-relevant teams quickly); log (non-PII) payment failure reasons to distinguish user error from systemic provider issues.
Synthetic monitoring/uptime checks specifically exercising the checkout flow on a schedule to catch silent breakages fast.
tradeoffs:
SSR/SSG vs. pure client-rendered SPA: choose SSR/SSG for the public catalog because SEO and first-paint performance materially affect revenue, but keep checkout/account as a simpler client-rendered SPA behind auth — don't over-engineer by SSR-ing pages where SEO doesn't matter, as that adds server infrastructure complexity for no benefit.
Start with a single monolithic frontend service layer per domain rather than GraphQL federation across catalog/cart/orders — only consider GraphQL if PDP composition genuinely requires stitching many independent services with divergent shapes, and the REST fan-out is causing measurable performance or maintenance pain.
Guest cart in localStorage vs. always-server cart: local storage is simpler and avoids extra backend calls for anonymous browsing, but sync to a server cart before checkout to avoid losing carts across devices — avoid building complex cross-device guest cart merging until analytics show it's a common enough scenario to justify it.
Avoid custom-building payment UI/logic; using a provider's hosted fields/SDK is both simpler and safer (PCI scope reduction) than a bespoke card-input solution — this is a clear case where "not reinventing the wheel" is the right call, not under-engineering.

→

→
Service Layer

→

followUpQuestions: How would you handle a flash sale where thousands of users hit the same product page simultaneously?
What happens if a user's payment succeeds at the provider but the confirmation request to your backend fails?
How would you keep cart state consistent if a user adds items on mobile and continues checkout on desktop?
How would you decide between SSR, SSG, and client-rendering for a specific page in this app?
How would you test that a discount code is applied correctly without letting the client control the final price?
spokenAnswer:
Start by clarifying scale, SEO importance, and whether this is single-seller or marketplace — that determines the rendering strategy for catalog pages.
Propose the route structure with SSR/SSG for public catalog/PDP pages (for SEO and Core Web Vitals) and a client-rendered SPA for cart/checkout/account behind auth, explaining why you're not SSR-ing everything uniformly.
Walk through component architecture (catalog grid/PDP/checkout-step components) and state ownership: server state cached via a query library, cart synced between guest local storage and server-side truth, minimal global state otherwise — flagging that you're deliberately not introducing Redux or GraphQL unless fan-out/aggregation pain actually shows up.
Spend real time on checkout as the highest-risk flow: idempotent submit, careful error handling for stock/payment races, and payment tokenization via a provider SDK so secret keys and raw card data never touch your frontend or backend directly.
Cover performance (image optimization, code-splitting checkout away from catalog), accessibility on forms, and monitoring focused on the purchase funnel and Core Web Vitals.
Close with your key trade-off — hybrid rendering over an all-SSR or all-CSR approach — and why that balance serves both SEO and simplicity without overengineering.

title: Design a real-time workflow application (WebSocket-driven task/approval dashboard)
clarifyingQuestions: What triggers real-time updates — task status changes, new approvals needed, comments, or all of the above?
How many concurrent users/connections per workspace, and how large can a single workflow board get (hundreds vs. thousands of tasks)?
Do we need multi-user collaboration on the same task/approval simultaneously (presence, live cursors), or just eventual consistency of state?
Is WebSocket infrastructure already in place, or could Server-Sent Events/polling be sufficient for the actual latency requirements?
What happens when a user is offline or the WebSocket drops — do we need offline queuing or is a reconnect-and-refetch acceptable?
Are there approval-chain/audit requirements (who approved what, in what order) that affect UI and data modeling?
functionalRequirements: Users see a live-updating board/list of tasks or approval requests without manual refresh
Users can perform actions (approve, reject, comment, reassign) that reflect instantly for themselves and near-instantly for others
Task/approval state changes show clear status and history/audit trail
Users are notified (in-app, and optionally push/email) when something needs their attention
Support filtering/sorting the live board (e.g., "my pending approvals") without breaking real-time updates
Reconnect gracefully after network loss and reconcile any missed updates
nonFunctionalRequirements: Updates should appear within a couple seconds of the underlying change for a "real-time" feel
Frontend must handle out-of-order or duplicate events from the WebSocket without corrupting local state
Graceful degradation to polling if WebSocket connection cannot be established (corporate proxies, etc.)
RBAC-aware — different users see different subsets/actions on the same underlying data, enforced server-side
Accessible live updates (screen reader users must be informed of important changes without being overwhelmed)
Resilient under reconnect storms (e.g., many clients reconnecting after a server deploy) without overloading the backend
routeStructure:
/workspace/:id/board            (main live task/approval board)
/workspace/:id/task/:taskId      (task detail with live comments/status)
/workspace/:id/approvals/mine    (filtered view: pending on me)
/workspace/:id/history           (audit trail, not real-time — paginated)
/workspace/:id/settings
/notifications                  (persistent notification center, cross-workspace)

The board and task-detail routes establish/maintain a WebSocket subscription scoped to that workspace; navigating away unsubscribes to avoid leaking connections.
componentArchitecture:
A WorkflowBoard component renders a list/kanban of TaskCard components, each reflecting live status; a TaskDetailPanel shows full history/comments for a selected task, updating in place as new events arrive.
A dedicated realtime layer (a hook like useWorkspaceSocket or a small "realtime client" module) owns the WebSocket connection, message parsing, and dispatches normalized events into the data layer (e.g., updating the query cache) — components never touch the raw socket.
ApprovalActionBar (approve/reject/comment controls) is a shared component reused in both the board's quick actions and the task detail view, driven by the current task's permitted actions from the backend rather than hardcoded per role.
NotificationCenter is a global, persistent component (bell icon + panel) subscribed to a lighter-weight "my notifications" event stream, decoupled from the heavier per-workspace board socket.
stateOwnership:
Server state (tasks, approvals, comments, history) is held in a normalized cache (e.g., React Query's cache, or a custom normalized store) keyed by entity ID so a single WebSocket event ("task 123 updated") can patch exactly that entity everywhere it's rendered, rather than refetching whole lists.
The WebSocket connection/subscription state (connected/reconnecting/disconnected) is separate, small global state consumed by a connection-status indicator and by logic that falls back to polling on prolonged disconnect.
UI-only state (which filter is active, which task is expanded, draft comment text) stays local to the relevant component.
Avoid pushing every incoming WebSocket message into one giant Redux-style store with manual reducers for every event type; instead, let events feed into the same cache your REST fetches populate, so there's one source of truth regardless of how data arrived (initial fetch vs. live update).
apiLayer:
Initial data load uses standard REST/GraphQL requests (fetch the board's current task list) through the normal service layer and query cache; the WebSocket is purely a stream of incremental "delta" events (task updated, comment added) that patch that same cache, not a replacement for the fetch layer.
Each event carries an entity type, ID, and version/timestamp so the client can apply it to the cache and detect out-of-order delivery (ignore an update older than what's already applied); a reconciliation fetch runs on reconnect to catch any events missed while disconnected.
Mutations (approve/reject) are still sent via normal HTTP requests to the API (not over the socket) for reliability/idempotency, and the resulting state change is broadcast to other clients via the server, which the frontend receives as just another incoming event.
authentication:
WebSocket connections authenticate using the same session (e.g., a short-lived token passed during the socket handshake, derived from the httpOnly session cookie) rather than a separate credential system.
Server-side, every event pushed to a client is filtered by that user's permissions (a client should never even receive an event for a workspace/task they can't see) — this is enforced on the backend's pub/sub layer, not by the frontend hiding data it already received.
Approval actions are re-validated server-side for permission and workflow-state correctness (e.g., can't approve out of order if the workflow requires sequential approval) regardless of what the frontend's optimistic UI shows.
errorHandling:
Optimistic updates for user-initiated actions (clicking "approve" instantly shows approved state) are rolled back with a clear inline error if the server rejects the action (e.g., someone else already approved/rejected it — a common race in approval workflows).
WebSocket disconnects show a subtle, non-alarming "reconnecting..." indicator rather than a jarring error, with automatic exponential-backoff reconnect; if reconnect fails repeatedly, fall back to periodic polling and show a clearer "live updates paused" notice.
Conflicting concurrent edits (two approvers acting on the same task at once) are resolved by trusting the server's authoritative state on the next event/reconciliation fetch, with a toast if the local optimistic view had to be corrected.
caching:
The normalized entity cache acts as the source of truth for rendering; WebSocket events and REST responses both write into it, so there's no separate "real-time cache" vs. "REST cache" to keep in sync.
History/audit trail pages (not real-time-critical) can use standard HTTP caching and pagination since they're read far less frequently and don't need live updates.
CDN caching applies normally to static assets; the live board itself is never HTTP-cached since it's inherently dynamic.
performance:
Batch/throttle UI updates from rapid-fire WebSocket events (e.g., coalesce multiple updates to the same task within a short window into one re-render) to avoid thrashing the DOM during bursts of activity.
Virtualize the task board/list when workspaces can have hundreds or thousands of tasks, so only visible TaskCards subscribe to re-renders.
Scope WebSocket subscriptions to what's currently visible (e.g., subscribe to a workspace's events only while its board is mounted) to avoid unnecessary bandwidth/CPU for background tabs or unrelated workspaces.
Debounce comment-typing indicators and other frequent low-value events rather than sending/processing every keystroke.
accessibility:
Live updates use polite aria-live regions for non-urgent status changes (task moved to "in review") and assertive regions sparingly for things needing immediate attention (a task was rejected and needs the user's action now) — avoid overwhelming screen reader users with a running commentary of every minor change.
The notification center and connection-status indicator are announced accessibly (not just a color-changing dot) and keyboard-navigable.
Approval actions have clear, non-color-only status indicators (icon + text: "Approved", "Rejected", "Pending") and confirmation before destructive actions like rejecting a request.
security:
WebSocket messages are treated as untrusted input from the network like any API response — never used to directly render raw HTML (sanitize any user-generated text like comments before rendering).
Authorization for both the initial socket handshake and every subsequent event is enforced server-side per user/workspace/task; the frontend never relies on "I just won't render events for workspaces I don't have open" as a security boundary.
Rate-limit and validate approval actions server-side to prevent replay or forged approval attempts, even if the frontend's optimistic UI briefly showed success.
testing:
Unit tests for the event-reconciliation logic (applying out-of-order/duplicate events to the cache correctly) since this logic is subtle and easy to get wrong.
Integration tests simulating a mocked WebSocket server sending a sequence of events and asserting the UI updates correctly, including reconnect-and-reconcile scenarios.
E2E tests for the core approval workflow across two simulated users/sessions (one approves, verify the other sees it update live) if feasible in the test environment, or at least mocked at the network layer.
Load/soak testing (often outside pure frontend scope, but coordinate with backend) to validate the UI stays responsive under high event throughput.
deployment:
Standard CDN-hosted frontend build; WebSocket endpoint is a separate backend concern but the frontend needs configuration for reconnect endpoints/regions and must handle backend deploys gracefully (server-initiated reconnect messages before a rolling restart).
Feature-flag any major real-time UX changes (e.g., switching from polling to WebSocket) to allow gradual rollout and quick rollback if connection issues appear in production.
Staging environment includes a realistic WebSocket setup (not just mocked) to catch connection/scaling issues before prod.
monitoring:
Track WebSocket connection health client-side (connect success rate, average reconnect time, fallback-to-polling rate) and report as metrics, since silent connection failures directly degrade the "real-time" value proposition.
Error tracking tagged with whether the error occurred during optimistic update rollback, event reconciliation, or normal API calls, to distinguish real-time-specific bugs from general ones.
Alert on anomalies like a sudden spike in fallback-to-polling clients, which often indicates a backend WebSocket infrastructure issue.
tradeoffs:
Start with simple polling (e.g., refetch every few seconds) if the real "real-time" requirement is actually just "reasonably fresh" — only invest in full WebSocket infrastructure and event-reconciliation logic once user research or SLAs demand sub-few-second latency; WebSockets add real complexity (connection lifecycle, reconnection, out-of-order events) that isn't worth it for a workflow tool where a 10-second staleness is fine.
Prefer patching a normalized entity cache from both REST and WebSocket sources over building a separate bespoke real-time store — this avoids two sources of truth and the synchronization bugs that come with it.
Optimistic UI is valuable for the primary approve/reject action but resist optimistically updating everything (e.g., don't optimistically reorder an entire list) — the added rollback complexity often isn't worth it for secondary interactions.
Consider Server-Sent Events instead of full-duplex WebSockets if the app only needs server-to-client push (approvals/status updates) without client-to-server streaming — SSE is simpler to implement and debug, and is a good example of choosing the least powerful tool that solves the actual problem.

Browser (Board UI)
↔
WebSocket Gateway
Normalized Entity Cache
←
REST API (initial load + actions)
Pub/Sub Backend
→
Workflow / Approval Service
followUpQuestions: How would you handle two approvers clicking "approve" on the same task within milliseconds of each other?
What is your strategy if the WebSocket connection is blocked entirely by a corporate firewall?
How do you avoid re-rendering the entire task board when only one task changes?
How would you test the event-reconciliation logic without a real WebSocket server?
At what point would you introduce presence/live-cursor features, and what would that add to the architecture?
spokenAnswer:
Begin by pinning down what "real-time" actually needs to mean here — latency tolerance and whether true bidirectional WebSockets are required, or whether SSE/polling would satisfy it more simply; this framing shows you don't reach for the heaviest tool by default.
Describe the route structure (board, task detail, filtered approvals-for-me, non-real-time history) and the component split, emphasizing that a dedicated realtime layer owns the socket and feeds events into the same normalized cache used by REST fetches — one source of truth, not two competing stores.
Explain how events carry IDs/versions so out-of-order or duplicate messages are handled safely, and how reconnect triggers a reconciliation fetch to catch anything missed.
Cover optimistic UI for the approve/reject action with rollback on server rejection, and stress that authorization and workflow-order rules are enforced server-side regardless of what the optimistic UI briefly shows.
Touch performance (throttling bursty updates, scoping subscriptions to visible workspaces, virtualizing large boards) and accessibility (careful use of aria-live so updates inform without overwhelming).
Finish with your trade-off: starting with simple polling or SSE unless sub-few-second latency is a real requirement, and only adopting full WebSocket complexity when that's justified — explicitly naming this as avoiding overengineering.

title: Design an ERP frontend (large tables, inventory, multi-module)
clarifyingQuestions: How many modules does the ERP cover (inventory, procurement, finance, HR) and are they used by mostly disjoint user groups?
What is the largest expected table size per module, and are there common operations like bulk edit/import/export across modules?
Do modules share a lot of data (e.g., an inventory item referenced in procurement and finance) requiring cross-module navigation/consistency?
Is this replacing an existing legacy ERP UI — are there specific power-user workflows (keyboard-heavy, dense grids) we must preserve?
What are the offline/unreliable-network requirements (e.g., warehouse floor devices with spotty wifi)?
Are there complex multi-step business processes (e.g., purchase-order approval chains) that span multiple modules?
functionalRequirements: Users can view, filter, sort, and paginate large datasets (inventory items, orders, transactions) across multiple modules
Users can perform inline edits and bulk operations (bulk update, import/export via CSV) on grid data
Cross-module linking — e.g., clicking an inventory item from a purchase order navigates to its inventory detail
Complex forms for creating/editing business entities (purchase orders, invoices) with validation and multi-step workflows
Role-based module access (e.g., warehouse staff sees inventory only, finance sees invoicing)
Reporting/export capability (generate and download reports from grid data)
nonFunctionalRequirements: Grids must stay responsive with tens of thousands of rows via virtualization and server-side operations
High data-entry efficiency — keyboard navigation and shortcuts for power users doing repetitive data entry
Strong data integrity — validation must prevent invalid business states before submission
Modular architecture so new modules can be added without destabilizing existing ones
Auditability — every change to business-critical records is tracked
Reasonable performance on internal corporate networks/older hardware, common in enterprise environments
routeStructure:
/erp                          (module launcher/home)
/erp/inventory                (item grid)
/erp/inventory/:id
/erp/procurement/purchase-orders
/erp/procurement/purchase-orders/:id
/erp/finance/invoices
/erp/finance/invoices/:id
/erp/reports/:reportId
/erp/admin/users-roles

Each module (inventory, procurement, finance, admin) is a separately lazy-loaded chunk since most users only work within one or two modules day-to-day; cross-module links (e.g., PO line item → inventory detail) navigate between chunks but load on demand.
componentArchitecture:
A shared DataGrid component (virtualized, server-paginated, sortable, inline-editable, supports column configuration) is the backbone of nearly every module — built once, configured per module via column/schema definitions rather than reimplemented per entity type.
A GenericEntityForm framework handles multi-step business forms (purchase order creation) with schema-driven validation, reused across modules with different field configs.
Each module is a self-contained feature folder (features/inventory, features/procurement) with its own routes, API calls, and grid/form configs, depending only on shared primitives (DataGrid, EntityForm, design-system components) — not on each other's internals, to keep modules independently maintainable.
A cross-module "entity link" component resolves references (e.g., an inventory item ID shown in a PO line) into a clickable link without each module needing to know the other's internal routing details, via a small shared registry/service.
stateOwnership:
Server state per module (inventory items, POs, invoices) is owned by a query/cache library scoped per module/entity type; modules do not share a single global data cache blindly, avoiding accidental coupling — instead cross-module reads (e.g., procurement needing inventory item names) go through explicit, scoped queries.
Global state is limited to session/user/role/permissions and perhaps active module/navigation context; each module keeps its own grid UI state (filters, sort, selected rows, in-progress edits) locally rather than centralizing it, since that state is meaningless outside the module.
Unsaved form/grid edits (critical in data-entry-heavy ERP flows) are tracked locally with a "dirty" flag and prompt-before-navigate-away protection, and optionally persisted to local storage as an autosave draft to protect against accidental data loss.
apiLayer:
Service layer organized per module/domain with a consistent contract (list with filters/sort/pagination params, get, create, update, bulkUpdate, export) so the shared DataGrid can be wired to any module's service with minimal glue code.
Bulk operations (import/export, bulk edit) are handled as asynchronous jobs on the backend when datasets are large (submit job, poll or receive a completion event) rather than blocking the UI on a giant synchronous request.
Cross-module reference resolution (e.g., batch-fetching item names for a page of PO lines) uses batched/dataloader-style requests to avoid N+1 API calls from the frontend.
authentication:
Session-based auth with role/permission sets scoped per module (e.g., warehouse-staff role grants inventory read/write but no finance access); nav and module launcher only show modules the user's role includes.
Field-level or row-level permission nuances (e.g., a regional manager can only edit inventory for their region) are still enforced server-side on every request — the frontend may hide/disable fields for UX clarity, but must never be the only barrier, since ERP data is often business/financially sensitive.
Sensitive modules (finance, admin) may require additional session verification (shorter session timeout, step-up auth) given the sensitivity of the data.
errorHandling:
Grid-level errors (a single row fails to save during bulk edit) are surfaced per-row rather than failing the entire batch silently — users see exactly which rows succeeded/failed and why, critical for trust in bulk operations.
Form validation errors are shown inline, tied to specific fields, with business-rule violations (e.g., "cannot exceed available stock") clearly distinguished from simple format errors.
Module-level error boundaries mean a bug in the reporting module doesn't take down inventory; a global fallback catches truly unexpected crashes with an option to reload without losing unsaved work where technically possible (e.g., restoring from an autosaved draft).
caching:
Reference/lookup data (categories, unit types, currency lists) that changes rarely is cached client-side with long staleTime/local persistence, since it's fetched constantly across nearly every module's forms and grids.
Grid data itself uses short staleTime given multi-user concurrent edits are common in ERP (someone else may have just updated a record) — favor revalidate-on-focus/interval over long caching for anything editable.
Exports/reports may be cached briefly if regenerating them is expensive, with a visible "generated at" timestamp so users know the data's freshness.
performance:
Virtualized grids are non-negotiable for ERP scale (tens of thousands of rows) — render only visible rows/columns, paginate/filter/sort server-side.
Code-split aggressively per module since ERP UIs tend to accumulate many modules over time, most of which a given user never touches in a session.
Debounce inline-edit autosave and batch multiple cell edits into fewer network requests where possible; use windowed rendering for wide grids with many columns (common in ERP) to avoid layout thrashing.
Lazy-load rarely used reporting/analytics widgets and heavy charting libraries only when the reports module is actually opened.
accessibility:
Data grids support full keyboard navigation (arrow keys between cells, Enter to edit, Escape to cancel) since ERP power users often rely on keyboard-only data entry for efficiency — this is both an accessibility and a productivity requirement.
Form validation errors are announced via aria-live and associated with their fields; multi-step forms show clear progress and allow going back without losing entered data.
High information-density grids still maintain sufficient color contrast and don't rely on color alone to flag issues like negative stock or overdue invoices (pair with icons/text).
security:
Strict server-side authorization per module/row/field given the financially and operationally sensitive nature of ERP data; frontend role-based UI is a productivity/UX feature, never the security boundary.
Input validation both client-side (fast feedback) and server-side (source of truth) for all business rules, since ERP data integrity issues can have real financial consequences.
Audit logging of all create/update/delete actions with user attribution, viewable by admins, to support compliance and dispute resolution.
CSV import/export features sanitize and validate uploaded data server-side before it touches production data (never trust client-parsed CSV content as-is).
testing:
Unit tests for grid configuration logic (column defs, validation schemas) shared across modules, and for business-rule validation functions (e.g., stock/quantity checks).
Integration tests for the DataGrid's inline editing, bulk operations, and error-per-row display, since it's reused everywhere and a bug there is maximally impactful.
E2E tests for at least one full cross-module workflow (create a purchase order → approve it → see inventory update) since these end-to-end business processes are where integration bugs hide.
Regression tests around CSV import/export edge cases (malformed rows, encoding issues) given how error-prone bulk data operations tend to be.
deployment:
Modular deployment: consider a monorepo with independently versioned module packages even if shipped as one deployed app, so teams owning different modules (inventory vs. finance) can develop somewhat independently while still shipping one cohesive build initially.
Staged rollout per module via feature flags, since ERP changes can disrupt real business operations — a broken inventory grid mid-shift is costly, so canary rollouts and quick rollback paths matter more here than in many consumer apps.
Separate, realistic staging environment with production-scale data volumes to catch grid performance issues before they reach real users.
monitoring:
Performance monitoring specifically on grid interactions (time to render N rows, time to apply a filter) since grid responsiveness is the single biggest UX factor in ERP satisfaction.
Error tracking tagged by module and action type (bulk-edit failures vs. form-validation vs. navigation errors) to help the right team triage quickly in a multi-module system.
Usage analytics per module to guide where to invest in UX improvements (e.g., which module has the highest support-ticket rate).
tradeoffs:
Start with a shared, configurable DataGrid/EntityForm rather than premature "module federation" or microfrontends split per module — a single well-modularized SPA with code-splitting gets most of the isolation benefit without the operational overhead of independently deployed microfrontends; only move to true microfrontends once separate teams need independent deploy cadences and the coordination cost of one build has become a real bottleneck.
Prefer synchronous UI for small bulk operations and async job + polling/event only for genuinely large ones — building a generic async-job UI for every operation from day one is overengineering if most bulk edits are small in practice.
Keep cross-module data access explicit and scoped (module A calls a small API to resolve module B's references) rather than a single shared global entity cache spanning all modules — that coupling seems convenient early but makes each module harder to reason about and test independently as the ERP grows.
CSV import/export: build a straightforward client-side parser + server-side validation initially; only invest in a fully asynchronous background-job import pipeline once file sizes/volumes actually demand it.

Module Launcher Shell
Inventory Module
Procurement Module
Finance Module
Shared DataGrid / EntityForm
→
Per-Module Service Layer
→
