followUpQuestions: How would you design the shared DataGrid so it works for both a 10-column inventory list and a 40-column finance ledger without becoming unmanageable?
How do you handle a bulk edit of 5,000 rows where 12 of them fail validation?
How would you prevent two users from overwriting each other's edits on the same purchase order?
What would push you toward splitting this into microfrontends per module, and what would you need in place first?
How would you support a warehouse floor scanner device with poor/intermittent connectivity for inventory updates?
spokenAnswer:
Open by scoping which modules exist and how much they share data/users, since that determines how independent the modules can be.
Describe the module-launcher route structure with per-module lazy-loaded chunks, then focus on the core reusable building blocks: a configurable, virtualized DataGrid and a schema-driven EntityForm that every module configures rather than reimplements.
Explain state ownership — server state scoped per module via a query cache, minimal global state (session/role), local grid/form UI state with dirty-tracking and autosave to protect data entry — and note you're keeping cross-module data access explicit rather than one shared cache, to preserve module independence.
Cover the API layer's consistent per-module contract, async job handling for genuinely large bulk operations (not for everything), and stress that authorization and business-rule validation are enforced server-side given the financial/operational stakes of ERP data.
Hit performance (virtualization is non-negotiable at ERP scale) and accessibility (full keyboard grid navigation, which doubles as a power-user productivity feature).
Close with your key trade-off: a modular single SPA over microfrontends for now, naming the concrete signal — independent team deploy needs — that would justify revisiting that later, explicitly framing it as avoiding premature architectural complexity.

title: Design a notification system (in-app + toast + persistent notification center)
clarifyingQuestions: What notification sources exist (system events, mentions, workflow updates, marketing) and do they all need the same treatment?
Do notifications need to be real-time (pushed via WebSocket/SSE) or is periodic polling/on-load fetching acceptable?
Should notifications sync across multiple open tabs/devices (e.g., dismissing on one device marks it read everywhere)?
Do we need integration with browser push notifications or email/SMS as parallel channels, and how does read-state reconcile across channels?
What is the expected volume per user (a handful a day vs. hundreds), which affects whether we need grouping/digesting?
Are there different notification priorities/types requiring different UI treatment (critical alert vs. informational toast)?
functionalRequirements: Users see transient toast notifications for immediate, in-session events (e.g., "Saved successfully", "New message")
Users have a persistent notification center (bell icon + panel/page) listing historical notifications, read/unread state
Users can mark notifications as read/unread, individually or in bulk ("mark all as read")
Clicking a notification navigates to the relevant context (e.g., the task, message, or record it references)
Notification preferences let users control which types they receive and through which channel (in-app, email, push)
Unread count badge stays accurate across tabs/sessions
nonFunctionalRequirements: Toasts must not be intrusive or block interaction, and must auto-dismiss or be dismissible
Notification center must scale to hundreds/thousands of historical notifications via pagination, not loading all at once
Real-time delivery (if required) should degrade gracefully to polling on connection issues
Accessible to screen-reader and keyboard users, including that toasts don't trap or steal focus disruptively
Consistent state across multiple open tabs of the same app
Low performance overhead — notification polling/sockets shouldn't degrade the rest of the app
routeStructure:
Notification UI is mostly a cross-cutting overlay rather than its own route tree:
/notifications                  (full page: paginated, filterable history)
/notifications/settings         (preferences per type/channel)

The toast layer and notification bell/panel are rendered globally from the AppShell (present on every authenticated route), not tied to a specific route, so notifications work regardless of where the user currently is in the app.
componentArchitecture:
ToastContainer is a single globally-mounted component (portal-rendered to avoid z-index/layout issues) that renders a queue of ToastItem components, each auto-dismissing after a timeout unless hovered/focused.
NotificationBell + NotificationPanel (dropdown) show a short recent list with unread indicators; a separate NotificationCenterPage handles the full paginated history with filters (by type, read/unread).
A central NotificationService/store manages the canonical list of notifications, unread count, and read-state — both the toast layer and the bell/panel subscribe to it rather than maintaining separate copies, so an incoming notification can simultaneously trigger a toast and update the persistent list without duplicated logic.
A declarative API for triggering notifications (e.g., notify({ type, message, entityRef }) callable from anywhere in the app) decouples feature code from the notification UI implementation.
stateOwnership:
The canonical notification list and unread count are server state, owned by a query/cache layer, kept fresh via periodic refetch, WebSocket/SSE push, or on window focus — not duplicated into a separate hand-rolled global store.
Toast queue state (which toasts are currently visible, their timers) is genuinely ephemeral client/UI state, local to the ToastContainer, since toasts don't need to survive a refresh or sync across tabs.
Cross-tab consistency (read-state, unread count) is handled via a shared source of truth (server) plus a lightweight cross-tab sync mechanism (BroadcastChannel or storage events) so marking as read in one tab updates the badge in others without each tab independently polling excessively.
apiLayer:
A notifications service (notifications.ts) wraps: listNotifications(pagination/filters), markRead(id | 'all'), and getUnreadCount, plus a subscribe mechanism (WebSocket/SSE) for push-based delivery if real-time is required.
Mark-as-read calls are optimistic (UI updates instantly) with rollback on failure, since this is a low-risk, frequent action where perceived responsiveness matters more than waiting for server confirmation.
If polling is used instead of push, the polling interval adapts (more frequent when the tab is focused/active, backed off when hidden) to balance freshness against unnecessary load.
authentication:
Notifications are strictly scoped to the authenticated user's session; the backend must never include another user's notifications in any response, and the frontend trusts but doesn't re-derive that scoping — no client-side filtering of "whose" notifications these are, since that would be a security anti-pattern if the backend ever mis-scoped a response.
Notification preferences are tied to the user's account and require authentication to view/change; changes take effect on the backend which is the actual enforcement point for what gets sent (e.g., suppressing emails), not just a frontend toggle.
errorHandling:
A failed fetch of the notification list shows a small inline retry affordance in the panel rather than a disruptive full-page error, since notifications are important but not typically blocking.
A failed "mark as read" optimistically reverts the read-state and shows a subtle toast/error indicator, without losing the user's place in the panel.
If real-time delivery fails/disconnects, fall back silently to polling rather than surfacing a scary error to the user — notification delivery being slightly delayed is a low-severity degradation, not a crash-worthy one.
caching:
The notification list uses short staleTime (frequently refreshed) given its time-sensitive nature, but historical/read notifications beyond the first page can be cached longer since they rarely change once read.
Unread count is cheap to keep fresh via a lightweight dedicated endpoint/event rather than recomputing from the full list, avoiding the need to fetch full notification bodies just to update a badge number.
No aggressive HTTP caching on notification endpoints given their per-user, frequently-changing nature; static assets (icons in the panel) are cached normally via CDN.
performance:
The notification history page virtualizes/paginates rather than rendering an ever-growing list; the dropdown panel shows only a small recent slice (e.g., last 10-20) with a "view all" link to the full paginated page.
Toast rendering is lightweight and capped (e.g., max 3-4 visible at once, queuing the rest) to avoid overwhelming the viewport and the DOM with excessive simultaneous animations.
If using WebSocket/SSE for push, the connection is shared/reused across the app (not one socket per component) to avoid redundant connections; polling-based fallback uses a sensible interval, not aggressive sub-second polling.
accessibility:
Toasts are announced via an aria-live="polite" region so screen readers announce new notifications without interrupting current focus/reading, and critical/urgent toasts can use assertive sparingly; toasts never steal keyboard focus automatically.
The notification bell shows unread count in a way that's programmatically associated (aria-label like "Notifications, 3 unread") not just a visual badge.
The notification panel and history page are fully keyboard-navigable (arrow keys or tab order through items, Enter to activate, clear focus indicators), and "mark all as read" is reachable and clearly labeled for assistive tech.
security:
Notification content (which may include user-generated text like a mention message) is sanitized/escaped before rendering to prevent stored XSS via notification payloads.
Deep links inside notifications are validated to point only to legitimate in-app routes/resources (avoid open-redirect patterns where a notification payload could be crafted to link externally in a misleading way).
No sensitive data (full payment details, secrets) should ever be included in notification payloads/content shown in the UI or push notifications, since these can appear on lock screens or in less secure contexts.
testing:
Unit tests for the notification store/service (dedup logic, unread count computation, optimistic mark-read with rollback).
Component tests for ToastContainer (queueing/dismissal behavior, max visible cap) and NotificationPanel (pagination, filters, empty state).
Integration tests simulating a push event arriving and verifying it updates both the toast layer and the persistent list/badge consistently.
Accessibility-focused tests verifying aria-live announcements fire appropriately and toasts don't hijack focus.
deployment:
Notification UI ships as part of the main app bundle (it's cross-cutting, used everywhere) but the store/service module should be small and tree-shakeable if unused notification types exist per product tier.
If using WebSocket/SSE, ensure the frontend handles backend deploys/restarts gracefully (reconnect logic) so a routine backend deploy doesn't visibly break notifications for users mid-session.
Feature flag new notification types/channels to roll out gradually and monitor for unexpected volume/noise before full release.
monitoring:
Track delivery-to-display latency for push-based notifications to catch systemic delays; track toast dismissal vs. click-through rates to understand whether notifications are useful or just noise.
Error tracking on notification fetch/mark-read failures, and monitoring for abnormal notification volume per user (could indicate a backend bug spamming notifications).
Monitor WebSocket/SSE connection health specifically for the notification channel if it's separate from other real-time features.
tradeoffs:
Start with polling (refetch on interval + on window focus) for the notification badge/list unless there's a clear, validated need for instant push delivery — polling is dramatically simpler to build/debug/scale and is often "real-time enough" for notifications (unlike, say, a live collaborative editor).
Keep a single NotificationService/store as the source of truth for both toasts and the persistent center rather than building two separate systems that happen to look similar — this avoids duplicated logic and inconsistent unread counts, without needing a heavyweight state library; plain context + a query cache is usually sufficient.
Cross-tab sync via BroadcastChannel/storage events is a lightweight addition; avoid overengineering this into a full multi-tab coordination protocol unless user research shows multi-tab usage is actually common enough to justify it — for many products, slightly stale badges across tabs until next poll is an acceptable trade-off.
Resist adding notification "digesting/grouping" logic (e.g., "5 new comments" summarization) until volume data shows individual notifications are actually overwhelming users — building that complexity upfront without evidence is premature.
diagramHtml:
App Shell
→
Notification Store
Toast Container
Bell / Panel
History Page
Notifications Service (poll/push)
→
Notification Backend
followUpQuestions: How would you keep the unread badge in sync across five open tabs of the same account?
How would you prevent a burst of 50 simultaneous notifications from overwhelming the toast UI?
How would you decide between polling and WebSocket push for this specific product?
How would you test that a notification's deep link correctly navigates to the right in-app resource?
How would you handle notification preferences so a user who disables email still sees in-app notifications?
spokenAnswer:
Start by clarifying volume, real-time expectations, and whether cross-tab/multi-channel sync actually matters for this product — that scopes how much infrastructure is justified.
Describe the architecture as a single NotificationService/store acting as source of truth, with the toast layer and the persistent bell/panel/history page all subscribing to it rather than maintaining separate state — this avoids duplicated logic and inconsistent counts.
Explain the default choice of polling (with focus-aware interval adjustment) over WebSocket push unless there's a validated need for instant delivery, framing this explicitly as avoiding overengineering until evidence justifies the added complexity.
Cover optimistic mark-as-read with rollback, graceful fallback if real-time delivery fails, and pagination/virtualization for the history page so it scales to large notification volumes.
Hit accessibility specifically — aria-live announcements for toasts without stealing focus, and full keyboard access to the panel — since notifications are a commonly under-accessible pattern.
Close with your trade-offs: polling over push by default, one shared store over two parallel systems, and holding off on grouping/digesting logic until real usage data shows it's needed.

title: Design a payment and checkout experience (Stripe/Razorpay style, without exposing secret keys)
clarifyingQuestions: Which payment methods must be supported (cards, wallets, bank transfers, buy-now-pay-later) and in which regions?
Is this a one-time checkout or does it also need to support saved payment methods/subscriptions?
Which payment provider(s) are in play, and do they offer hosted/embedded UI components (Stripe Elements, Razorpay Checkout) we should build on rather than a custom card form?
What compliance requirements apply (PCI DSS scope, SCA/3D Secure in certain regions)?
Should checkout support guest users, or is an account required?
What is the acceptable failure/retry UX — can a user retry with a different payment method seamlessly if one fails?
functionalRequirements: User enters/selects a payment method and submits payment for an order/subscription
Support saved payment methods for returning users (tokenized, not raw card storage)
Handle payment confirmation flows including 3D Secure/step-up authentication redirects
Show clear success/failure/pending states, with retry on failure using a different method
Display order summary/receipt after successful payment
Support refunds/cancellations initiation from the user side where applicable (e.g., cancel a subscription)
nonFunctionalRequirements: No raw card/payment credential data ever touches application code — PCI scope minimized via provider-hosted fields/SDKs
No secret API keys are ever present in frontend code or bundles — only publishable/public keys
High reliability — payment flow must handle network interruptions without double-charging or losing the user's progress
Accessible payment forms (critical since payment failures/friction disproportionately affect users relying on assistive tech)
Fast, low-friction flow — every added field/step measurably reduces conversion
Auditable — every payment attempt/outcome is logged for reconciliation and support
routeStructure:
/checkout                     (order summary, entry point)
/checkout/payment             (payment method selection + provider-hosted fields)
/checkout/processing          (transient state while confirming/3DS redirect)
/checkout/success             (confirmation + receipt)
/checkout/failed              (clear failure reason + retry CTA)
/account/payment-methods      (manage saved methods, tokenized)
/account/subscriptions        (manage recurring payments)

The payment step itself often renders the provider's hosted iframe/Elements directly within /checkout/payment rather than a fully custom form, and 3D Secure redirects return to /checkout/processing to finalize state.
componentArchitecture:
A CheckoutFlow controller component coordinates steps (summary → payment → confirmation) and holds only non-sensitive state (selected saved method ID, order ID) — never raw card data, which lives entirely inside the payment provider's embedded iframe/component and never enters the app's own component tree or state.
PaymentMethodSelector lists saved methods (masked, e.g., "Visa ****4242") plus an option for a new method, which mounts the provider's hosted card element (Stripe Elements/Razorpay Checkout) — a well-isolated wrapper component so the rest of the app doesn't need to know the provider's SDK details.
OrderSummary and ReceiptView are simple presentational components reused across the summary and success pages.
A PaymentStatusPoller/listener component handles the "processing" state, polling or listening for the backend's confirmation of payment status after redirect-based flows (3DS) complete.
stateOwnership:
Non-sensitive checkout state (selected saved payment method, current step, order ID, applied discount code) is local/session state in the checkout flow — persisted to sessionStorage so a page refresh or 3DS redirect-and-return doesn't lose progress.
Raw payment credential data (card number, CVV) is never held in the application's own state at all — it lives exclusively inside the payment provider's hosted iframe, which the app cannot and should not read; the app only ever receives a non-sensitive token/payment-method ID back from the provider's SDK.
Payment outcome/status (succeeded, failed, requires_action) is server state — fetched/confirmed from the backend, which itself received the authoritative result from the payment provider via webhook, not solely trusted from client-side redirect parameters.
apiLayer:
The frontend calls the app's own backend to create a "payment intent"/order on the server (this is where the provider's secret key is used, server-side only); the backend returns a client secret or session ID that the frontend passes to the provider's SDK to mount the hosted payment UI.
After the user submits payment via the provider's SDK (client-side), the SDK handles submitting card data directly to the provider (never through the app's own backend), returning a result the frontend then confirms with the app's backend to finalize the order.
The backend also listens for the payment provider's webhooks as the authoritative source of truth for payment success/failure (since client-side confirmation can be interrupted or spoofed) — the frontend's job is to reflect that server-confirmed state, polling or refetching order status rather than declaring success purely from a client-side callback.
authentication:
Checkout works for both guest sessions (session-scoped order, no login required) and authenticated users (who can save methods for reuse); saved payment methods are tied to the authenticated user's account and require login to view/manage.
All payment-method management endpoints (view saved methods, delete a method) are authorized server-side to ensure a user can only see/modify their own tokenized methods — the frontend never has access to raw method details beyond the masked display data the backend chooses to return.
Sensitive account actions (adding/removing a payment method, viewing full billing history) may warrant re-authentication (password/MFA re-entry) as an extra layer, enforced server-side.
errorHandling:
Every failure mode gets a specific, actionable message: card declined (retry with different method), 3DS authentication failed/cancelled (retry), network interruption mid-payment (check status before assuming failure — never blindly retry a charge without checking if it already succeeded), and generic provider errors (fallback message with support contact).
Idempotency keys are used when creating/confirming a payment/order so that a retried request due to a network blip doesn't create a duplicate charge.
The "processing" state explicitly handles the case where the user closes the tab or loses connection mid-3DS-redirect — on return/next visit, the app checks order status from the backend rather than assuming failure and prompting a re-attempt that could double-charge.
caching:
Payment and order data are never cached via standard HTTP caching (Cache-Control: no-store) given their sensitivity and volatility; nothing about card details is ever stored client-side (including in caches, localStorage, or logs).
Static checkout page assets (non-sensitive UI chrome) can be cached/CDN-served normally; the provider's SDK script itself is typically loaded from the provider's own CDN per their integration guide (not self-hosted, both for correctness and because provider SDKs are updated for security patches).
Saved payment method lists (masked display data only) can be cached briefly client-side like any other user data, invalidated on add/remove.
performance:
Load the payment provider's SDK script asynchronously and only on the checkout/payment step, not on every page, to avoid unnecessary payload on pages that don't need it.
Minimize the number of checkout steps/fields — every additional required field or page load in the flow is a measurable conversion risk, so keep the critical path (summary → payment → confirm) as short as reasonably possible.
Preload/prefetch the next likely step (e.g., start initializing the payment intent as soon as the user reaches checkout, before they finish reviewing the order) to reduce perceived latency at the payment step.
accessibility:
Because the actual card input fields are rendered inside the provider's hosted iframe, accessibility of those specific fields depends on the provider's implementation — choose a provider/integration known for accessible hosted fields (most major providers support this) rather than building a custom card form that reinvents accessible input masking/validation.
Surrounding UI (payment method selection, order summary, error messages, retry buttons) is fully keyboard-operable with clear focus order across the flow, and errors are announced via aria-live tied to the relevant step.
Success/failure/processing states are clearly conveyed to screen readers, not just via a visual spinner or checkmark icon.
security:
Never handle raw card data in application code — always use the payment provider's hosted fields/SDK (PCI DSS SAQ A scope) rather than a custom form, which would put the app in a much stricter PCI compliance scope with correspondingly higher security burden.
Only the publishable/public key is present in the frontend; the secret key lives exclusively server-side and is used only for backend-to-provider API calls (creating intents, confirming charges, processing refunds) — this cannot be stressed enough as the single most important rule of this design.
Validate and finalize payment/order state from the backend's webhook-confirmed truth, never trusting a client-side "success" callback alone, since a malicious client could attempt to spoof a success redirect without actually completing payment.
All checkout traffic is served over HTTPS (non-negotiable), with CSP configured to allow the payment provider's required script/frame origins while restricting everything else.
testing:
Unit tests for checkout flow state transitions (step progression, retry logic) and for idempotency-key generation/usage.
Integration tests using the payment provider's official test-mode/sandbox (test card numbers, simulated declines and 3DS challenges) to validate every documented failure/success path without real charges.
E2E tests covering the full happy path plus at minimum: a declined card retried successfully, a 3DS challenge completed, and a network interruption mid-flow that resolves correctly on return.
Manual/security review specifically checking that no secret keys, raw card data, or sensitive tokens ever appear in frontend bundles, network requests to non-provider domains, or client-side logs.
deployment:
Checkout changes go through extra scrutiny (staged rollout, feature flags, canary) given the direct revenue and trust impact of any regression; a broken checkout is one of the costliest possible frontend bugs.
Separate sandbox/test-mode provider credentials in staging so full checkout testing (including declines and 3DS) never touches real money.
Monitor deploys closely with an easy, fast rollback path specifically for the checkout module, potentially decoupled from the rest of the app's release cadence given its criticality.
monitoring:
Payment success/failure/abandonment rates are among the most business-critical metrics to monitor in real time, broken down by payment method and failure reason, to quickly catch systemic issues (e.g., a specific card network failing at unusually high rates).
Error tracking with high-priority alerting specifically for checkout-flow errors, and synthetic monitoring that periodically exercises the checkout path (using test-mode credentials) to catch silent breakages before real users do.
Log payment attempts and outcomes (non-sensitive metadata only — never card numbers) for reconciliation with the payment provider's own records and for customer support investigations.
tradeoffs:
Always use the payment provider's hosted fields/SDK over a custom-built card form — this isn't really a trade-off with two reasonable sides; the PCI scope reduction and security benefit are large enough that "build vs. use provider SDK" should default strongly to using the SDK unless there's an extremely unusual requirement.
Keep checkout state management simple (local/session state in the flow controller) rather than routing payment flow state through a heavyweight global store — checkout is usually a fairly linear, contained flow, and over-abstracting it into a generic global state machine framework is often unnecessary complexity for what's fundamentally a short wizard.
Prefer polling/refetching order status after a redirect-based 3DS flow over trying to maintain complex client-side state across the redirect — trusting the backend's webhook-confirmed truth is simpler and more correct than trying to reconstruct payment state purely client-side.
Don't build custom retry/idempotency logic beyond what's needed — most payment providers' SDKs and idempotency-key patterns already solve the double-charge problem; reinventing that logic client-side is both risky and usually unnecessary.

Checkout UI
→
Provider Hosted Fields (Elements/Checkout)
App Backend (creates intent, secret key here)
→
Payment Provider API
Provider Webhook
→
App Backend (confirms order)
→
Frontend (reflects final status)
followUpQuestions: Why should raw card data never touch your own frontend or backend code, and what does that actually reduce in terms of compliance burden?
How would you handle a user whose network drops right after submitting payment but before seeing a confirmation?
How do you prevent a double charge if a user double-clicks the "pay" button?
Why should you trust the payment provider's webhook over the client-side redirect result to mark an order as paid?
How would you extend this design to support saved payment methods for recurring subscription billing?
spokenAnswer:
Open with the single most important constraint: raw card data and secret API keys must never enter frontend code, so the design centers on the payment provider's hosted fields/SDK and a clear client/backend split of responsibilities.
Walk through the flow: the app's backend creates a payment intent using its secret key, returns a client secret to the frontend, which mounts the provider's hosted card UI and submits directly to the provider — the app's own state only ever holds non-sensitive identifiers like order ID and selected saved-method ID.
Explain why the backend's webhook, not the client-side redirect callback, is the authoritative source of payment success — this addresses a common failure mode where network drops or spoofed client state could otherwise cause incorrect order status.
Cover idempotency keys to prevent double charges, specific error handling per failure type (declined, 3DS failed, network interruption), and that checkout accessibility mostly depends on choosing a provider integration known for accessible hosted fields rather than building custom card inputs.
Touch monitoring (checkout is one of the highest-stakes flows to alert on) and deployment caution (staged rollout, fast rollback).
Close by naming the trade-off explicitly: using the provider's SDK over a custom form isn't really a trade-off, it's close to a "must," and keeping checkout state management simple/local rather than routing it through a global store or building a custom retry framework avoids unnecessary complexity in what's fundamentally a short, linear flow.

title: Design a reusable component library (design system) shared across products
clarifyingQuestions: How many products/teams will consume this library, and do they use the same framework/version (React 18 everywhere, or mixed)?
Is there an existing design language/Figma system to codify, or are we defining visual design and component API simultaneously?
What is the versioning/release cadence expectation — can consuming teams tolerate frequent breaking changes, or do we need strict semver and migration support?
Do we need theming support (multiple brands, light/dark mode) from day one?
How will the library be distributed — npm package(s), a monorepo with shared packages, or a hosted component registry?
What is the governance model — one central team owns it, or is it community-contributed across product teams?
functionalRequirements: Provide a core set of accessible, documented components (buttons, inputs, modals, tables, tooltips, etc.) usable across consuming apps
Support theming (tokens for color, spacing, typography) so different products can apply brand variations
Provide clear versioned releases with changelogs so consumers can safely upgrade
Include a documentation/playground site (e.g., Storybook) showing usage, props, and accessibility notes per component
Support tree-shaking so consumers only bundle the components they actually use
Provide composition primitives (not just fixed components) for cases where teams need custom layouts
nonFunctionalRequirements: Components must meet WCAG 2.1 AA by default so consuming teams don't have to re-solve accessibility per product
Backward compatibility within a major version — breaking changes are opt-in via major version bumps with migration guides
Small bundle footprint per component, with no unnecessary shared runtime bloat for consumers using only a few components
Well-tested (visual regression + unit + a11y tests) since regressions here ripple across every consuming product
Framework-agnostic where feasible at the design-token level, even if components themselves target a specific framework
Fast local dev feedback loop for contributors (fast Storybook builds, hot reload)
routeStructure:
Not an end-user app route structure, but the documentation/dev site follows a similar pattern:
/docs                         (getting started, installation)
/docs/foundations/colors      (design tokens)
/docs/foundations/typography
/docs/components/button       (props table, usage examples, a11y notes)
/docs/components/data-table
/docs/patterns/forms          (composed patterns built from primitives)
/docs/changelog

The library itself is published as versioned packages (e.g., @org/ui-core, @org/ui-icons, @org/ui-tokens) rather than "routes," consumed via imports in downstream apps.
componentArchitecture:
Split into layered packages: a tokens package (colors, spacing, typography as design tokens, framework-agnostic — e.g., JSON/CSS variables), a primitives/core package (unstyled or minimally-styled accessible building blocks: Button, Dialog, Tooltip, built on solid accessibility foundations, potentially via a headless UI library), and a styled components package that applies the design system's visual language on top of the primitives.
Each component exposes a small, composable API (e.g., a Modal that accepts children/slots for header/body/footer rather than dozens of specific props) so consuming teams can adapt layout without needing new component variants for every use case.
Complex components (DataTable, DatePicker) are built from the same shared primitives (e.g., Popover, Button) used elsewhere, avoiding duplicated logic across the library itself.
Storybook (or similar) serves as both documentation and the primary development/testing environment, with stories doubling as visual regression test fixtures.
stateOwnership:
As a library, most components should be as stateless/controlled as possible by default (value + onChange props) so consuming apps own the actual state and integrate the component into their own state management approach — the library shouldn't assume or impose how consumers manage state.
Where internal state is unavoidable (e.g., a dropdown's open/closed state), provide both an uncontrolled default (component manages its own state) and a controlled override (consumer can pass open/onOpenChange) so both simple and advanced use cases are supported without forcing complexity on basic consumers.
Theme state (current theme/brand) is provided via a context/provider at the app root that all components read from, so consuming apps set it once rather than passing theme props through every component.
apiLayer:
A component library typically has no API layer of its own — but do include patterns/hooks for common integration points (e.g., a useAsyncSelect hook pattern for a Select component that needs to fetch options) documented as recommended patterns rather than baked-in fetching logic, since data-fetching approaches vary by consuming app.
Where the library does include data-oriented components (like a DataTable), keep data-fetching entirely outside the component (it receives rows/columns as props and emits events like onSortChange/onPageChange) so it stays agnostic to whichever API layer or query library each consuming product uses.
authentication: The component library itself is typically auth-agnostic — it has no concept of users/sessions. However, if it includes any components that touch sensitive contexts (e.g., a shared "permission gate" wrapper component), ensure documentation is explicit that such a component only controls rendering/UX and that all real authorization must still be enforced by each consuming app's backend — the library must not create a false sense of security by looking like an auth boundary.
errorHandling:
Components should fail gracefully with clear, actionable prop-validation errors in development (e.g., PropTypes/TypeScript errors, runtime warnings for misuse) but never throw uncaught in production in a way that could crash a consuming app's entire page — validate critical invariants and degrade to a safe fallback render where feasible.
Provide guidance/an example for how consuming apps should wrap library components with their own error boundaries, since the library can't own error-boundary placement in someone else's app tree.
Any internal async behavior (e.g., a component that lazy-loads an icon set) handles its own failure states (fallback icon) rather than propagating an unhandled rejection.
caching:
Not typically applicable in the traditional HTTP-caching sense, but package publishing should use immutable versioned releases (never mutate a published version) so consumers' own build caches and CDNs can safely cache specific versions indefinitely.
If the library ships a hosted documentation site, that site itself benefits from standard CDN/static-asset caching like any other static site.
Consumers should be guided to use tree-shaking-friendly imports (import { Button } from '@org/ui') so their bundlers can cache/optimize per-component rather than pulling in the whole library.
performance:
Ensure the library supports tree-shaking (ES modules, sideEffects: false where accurate) so a consumer using three components doesn't pay for the whole library's bundle size.
Avoid bundling heavy dependencies (large date libraries, full icon sets) into the core package by default — offer them as optional peer dependencies or separate sub-packages (e.g., @org/ui-icons) so consumers opt in only to what they need.
Measure and publish bundle-size budgets per component (tracked in CI) so size regressions are caught before release, since bundle bloat here multiplies across every consuming product.
accessibility:
Accessibility is a first-class, non-negotiable requirement of the library itself — every interactive component (Button, Dialog, Menu, Tooltip, Tabs) implements correct ARIA roles/attributes, keyboard interaction patterns (per WAI-ARIA APG), and focus management (e.g., focus trap in modals, focus restoration on close) out of the box, so consuming teams inherit accessibility rather than each having to solve it themselves.
Automated accessibility testing (axe-core integrated into component tests/CI) runs on every component, and manual screen-reader testing is part of the release checklist for new/changed interactive components.
Documentation explicitly calls out accessibility usage requirements (e.g., "always provide an aria-label if using icon-only buttons") since misuse by consumers can still break accessibility even with a well-built component.
security:
Components must safely handle untrusted content passed in as props (e.g., a Tooltip or Card rendering user-generated text) by defaulting to safe text rendering rather than dangerouslySetInnerHTML, pushing the responsibility of sanitization to consumers only where they explicitly opt into rendering raw HTML (and documenting that risk clearly).
Dependencies are kept minimal and regularly audited (npm audit / Dependabot) since a vulnerability in a widely-used shared library has an outsized blast radius across every consuming product.
Never embed any environment-specific secrets, keys, or endpoints in the library itself — it should be entirely environment-agnostic and configuration-free regarding anything sensitive.
testing:
Unit tests for component logic/behavior (state transitions, keyboard interactions, controlled/uncontrolled behavior).
Automated accessibility tests (axe) integrated into the same test suite/CI pipeline as functional tests, treated as blocking, not optional.
Visual regression tests (e.g., via Chromatic or similar, built on Storybook stories) to catch unintended visual changes across the huge surface area of a design system.
Consumer-facing integration smoke tests (or a canary consuming app in CI) that installs the latest library build and verifies core flows still work, catching breaking changes before they reach real consuming products.
deployment:
Published as versioned npm packages following strict semantic versioning; a clear, automated changelog (e.g., via changesets) documents every release, with migration guides for major/breaking versions.
CI pipeline: lint, typecheck, unit + a11y + visual regression tests, then automated publish on merge to a release branch, gated by required passing checks given the wide blast radius of a bad release.
A documentation/Storybook site is deployed alongside each release (versioned docs) so consumers can reference the exact docs matching the version they've installed, not just "latest."
monitoring:
Track adoption/usage metrics (which components/versions are used across consuming products, via package analytics or internal telemetry) to guide deprecation decisions and prioritize maintenance.
Monitor bundle-size trends over time per component/release to catch creeping bloat before it becomes a widespread problem across consumers.
Collect structured feedback/issue reports from consuming teams (a lightweight internal issue tracker or shared channel) to catch usability/accessibility gaps that automated tests miss.
tradeoffs:
Start with a single well-organized package (or a small number of packages: tokens, core, icons) rather than over-splitting into dozens of micro-packages per component from day one — excessive package fragmentation adds publishing/versioning overhead that isn't justified until the library and its consumer base are large enough to need that granularity.
Prefer building on a solid headless/accessible primitives foundation (or a well-maintained headless UI library) rather than hand-rolling every accessibility behavior (focus trapping, ARIA patterns) from scratch — reinventing these is both risky and a poor use of a small team's time versus building the styled layer on top of a proven foundation.
Don't force a single global state-management pattern onto consumers; keep components controlled/uncontrolled-flexible rather than, say, requiring every consumer to adopt a specific global store just to use a Select component — that would needlessly constrain very different consuming apps.
Avoid premature multi-framework support (e.g., building React AND Vue AND Angular versions simultaneously) unless there's already a confirmed multi-framework consumer base — start with the framework the majority of products use, and only invest in cross-framework tokens/wrappers once there's real, not hypothetical, demand.

spokenAnswer:
Start by clarifying scale — how many consuming products/teams, whether they share a framework, and what the governance/versioning expectations are, since that shapes how strict you need to be about API stability.
Describe the layered package architecture: framework-agnostic design tokens, accessible headless-style primitives, and a styled component layer built on top — explaining why building on solid accessible primitives beats hand-rolling ARIA/focus-management logic per component.
Cover component API design: controlled/uncontrolled flexibility so the library doesn't impose a state-management opinion on consumers, and composable slot-based APIs over rigid prop explosions.
Explain accessibility as a first-class, CI-enforced requirement (automated axe tests, keyboard interaction patterns) since this is the single biggest value-add of a shared library — consuming teams inherit it instead of re-solving it.
Touch performance (tree-shaking, avoiding bundled heavy dependencies) and release process (strict semver, changelogs, visual regression testing given the wide blast radius of any regression).
Close with your trade-offs: starting with a small number of well-organized packages rather than over-fragmenting, and deliberately not building multi-framework support or forcing a state-management pattern until real, confirmed demand exists — framing this as protecting a small team's leverage rather than over-building speculative flexibility.

title: Design an authentication and RBAC architecture (explicitly note backend enforcement is mandatory)
clarifyingQuestions: What auth methods are required — email/password, SSO/OAuth, magic links, MFA — and are there enterprise SSO requirements (SAML/OIDC)?
Is this a single application or multiple products sharing one identity provider (requiring SSO across products)?
How granular does RBAC need to be — coarse roles (admin/user) or fine-grained permissions (per-resource, per-action)?
Do permissions ever need to be resource-scoped (e.g., "editor of project X" rather than a global role)?
What are session/token expiry and refresh requirements, and is there a need for "remember me" or persistent sessions across devices?
Are there compliance requirements (SOC 2, GDPR) affecting session handling, audit logging, or data access?
functionalRequirements: Users can register/log in via supported methods (password, SSO, etc.) and log out, ending their session everywhere if needed
Users can reset forgotten passwords and optionally enable MFA
The frontend renders UI (nav, buttons, pages) conditionally based on the current user's role/permissions
Unauthorized access attempts (navigating to a route/action the user lacks permission for) are handled gracefully (redirect/403 page)
Session persists appropriately across page reloads and expires/refreshes according to policy
Admins can manage other users' roles/permissions through an admin UI
nonFunctionalRequirements: All authorization is enforced server-side; frontend RBAC is strictly a UX/convenience layer, never a security boundary
Tokens/session data are stored securely (httpOnly cookies preferred over localStorage) to reduce XSS-based token theft risk
Session/token refresh happens transparently without disrupting the user's workflow
Auth flows are accessible (screen-reader-friendly forms, clear error messaging, keyboard-operable MFA input)
Scales to fine-grained, resource-scoped permissions without the frontend needing a full permissions matrix hardcoded per page
Resilient to auth-service outages with clear, non-cryptic messaging rather than silent failures
routeStructure:
/login
/signup
/forgot-password
/reset-password/:token
/mfa-challenge
/sso/callback                  (OAuth/SAML redirect handler)

/app/*                         (all authenticated routes, wrapped in a route guard)
/app/403                       (permission-denied fallback within the app)
/app/admin/users               (role/permission management, admin-only)

Route guards check authentication status (redirect to /login if unauthenticated) and, separately, permission checks per route (redirect to /app/403 if authenticated but lacking the required permission) — these are two distinct checks, not conflated.
componentArchitecture:
An AuthProvider (context) at the app root exposes the current user, their roles/permissions, and auth actions (login, logout, refresh) to the rest of the app.
A <RequireAuth> route wrapper redirects unauthenticated users to login; a separate <RequirePermission permission="..."> wrapper (or a usePermission('...') hook) conditionally renders children or a fallback based on the current user's permissions — used both for whole routes and for smaller UI elements (hide/disable a button the user can't use).
An admin RoleManagementPage lets admins assign roles/permissions to users, built from the same shared DataTable/EntityForm primitives as other admin tooling rather than a bespoke one-off UI.
Login/signup/MFA forms are relatively simple, focused components with strong validation and clear error states, kept separate from the main app shell/bundle (loaded only pre-auth).
stateOwnership:
The authenticated user's identity and permission set is global state (needed everywhere) but should be sourced from a single place — typically fetched once on app load (or decoded from a validated session) and held in the AuthProvider context, not duplicated into multiple ad hoc stores.
Permission-check results derived from that state (e.g., "can this user edit this specific project") are computed on demand via a hook/selector rather than stored separately, since they're derived data, not independent state — avoiding the two getting out of sync.
Session/token refresh state (is a refresh in flight, last refresh time) is internal implementation detail of the auth layer, not exposed as general app state.
apiLayer:
An auth service (auth.ts) wraps login, logout, refreshSession, and getCurrentUser/permissions calls; other service calls (e.g., orders.ts, users.ts) go through a shared HTTP client configured to automatically attach credentials (cookies) and handle 401s by attempting a silent refresh (or redirecting to login if refresh fails) transparently, so individual feature code doesn't need to handle auth-expiry logic itself.
Permission data is fetched as part of session/user bootstrap (not re-fetched per route) but the frontend must treat this as advisory for UX purposes only — every sensitive API call is independently authorized by the backend regardless of what the frontend believes the user's permissions are.
For resource-scoped permissions (e.g., "editor on project X"), the frontend can either fetch a permissions summary per resource when loading that resource's detail view, or rely on the backend returning 403s for specific actions and handling that gracefully rather than trying to precompute a full permission matrix client-side.
authentication:
Prefer httpOnly, secure, SameSite cookies for session tokens over storing JWTs in localStorage/sessionStorage, since JavaScript-accessible token storage is vulnerable to theft via any XSS vulnerability elsewhere in the app — httpOnly cookies aren't readable by JS at all, meaningfully reducing that attack surface.
SSO/OAuth flows redirect to the identity provider and back via a callback route that exchanges the auth code for a session (ideally handled server-side to keep tokens out of the browser's URL/history where possible).
MFA challenge is a distinct, focused step in the login flow, not bolted on awkwardly; "remember this device" (if supported) is a deliberate, time-limited exception, not a way to bypass MFA indefinitely.
CRITICALLY: role/permission checks in the frontend (hiding a button, redirecting from a route) are exclusively a UX convenience — every single sensitive operation must be independently authorized by the backend on every request, since a user can trivially bypass any frontend check by calling the API directly. This point should be treated as non-negotiable in the design, not a minor footnote.
errorHandling:
Login/signup form errors are specific and helpful (wrong password vs. account not found vs. account locked) without leaking information that aids attackers (avoid confirming whether an email exists on a failed login attempt, for example — a security/UX trade-off worth naming explicitly).
Expired sessions trigger a silent token refresh attempt first; only if that fails does the app redirect to login, ideally preserving the user's current location so they land back where they were after re-authenticating.
Permission-denied errors from the backend (403s on actions the frontend thought were allowed — e.g., stale permission cache) show a clear "you don't have permission" message and trigger a refresh of the local permission state, rather than a confusing generic error.
caching:
The current user's session/permission data is cached in memory (context) for the session's duration but revalidated on key events (window focus after being away, before sensitive actions) since permissions can change server-side (e.g., an admin revokes a role) while the user is still active.
Auth-related API responses (login, token refresh) are never HTTP-cached (Cache-Control: no-store); static assets for the login page itself can be cached normally via CDN like any other static content.
Avoid caching permission-check results for long periods without revalidation — a stale "can edit" cached client-side after an admin revokes access is a real (if UX-only) staleness bug worth guarding against with reasonably short cache lifetimes or explicit invalidation on relevant events.
performance:
Auth/login pages are a separate, small bundle loaded before the user is authenticated, kept lean since it's often the very first thing a user waits on.
Permission checks used for conditional rendering should be cheap, synchronous lookups against already-fetched data (not a network call per check) to avoid introducing latency into routine UI rendering decisions.
Token refresh happens in the background without blocking the user's current interaction — a silent refresh should not, for example, freeze a form the user is actively filling out.
accessibility:
Login, signup, and password-reset forms have properly labeled fields, clear inline validation errors linked via aria-describedby, and are fully operable via keyboard including MFA code entry (avoid custom input widgets that break paste-from-authenticator-app or screen reader compatibility).
Permission-denied pages/messages are announced clearly (not just a silent redirect) so screen reader users understand why they landed where they did.
Session-expiry warnings (if implemented, e.g., "your session will expire in 2 minutes") are announced via aria-live with enough time and a clear action to extend the session.
security:
This entire design's central security principle: frontend authentication/RBAC logic exists purely to shape the user experience (what's shown, what's navigable) and must never be treated as the actual security boundary — the backend independently validates the authenticated user's identity and permissions on every single request, with no exceptions, since client-side code and state can always be inspected or manipulated.
Session tokens in httpOnly cookies to mitigate XSS-based theft; CSRF protection (SameSite cookies plus CSRF tokens on state-changing requests) since cookie-based auth is vulnerable to CSRF if not mitigated.
Rate-limit login/password-reset endpoints (backend-enforced) to mitigate brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks; never expose whether a specific email/username exists via differential error messages beyond what's necessary.
Any third-party auth/identity provider secrets (OAuth client secrets) live server-side only — only public client IDs are ever present in frontend code.
testing:
Unit tests for the permission-derivation logic (given a user's roles/permissions, what should usePermission return) since bugs here cause visible UX/security confusion even though the backend is the real gate.
Integration tests for route guards (unauthenticated → redirected to login; authenticated but unauthorized → redirected to 403; authenticated and authorized → renders correctly).
E2E tests for the full auth lifecycle: signup, login, MFA challenge, session expiry and silent refresh, logout, and an admin changing a user's role and that user's UI updating accordingly on next load/refresh.
Security-focused tests/review verifying no sensitive tokens leak into localStorage, URLs, or client-side logs, and that frontend permission checks are indeed backed by equivalent backend enforcement (often validated via a dedicated security review or pen test, not just unit tests).
deployment:
Auth-related code changes (login flow, token handling, permission logic) warrant extra review scrutiny and staged rollout given the security sensitivity, even more than typical feature changes.
Environment-specific OAuth/SSO client IDs and redirect URLs are configured per environment (dev/staging/prod) via public (non-secret) build-time config; secrets for the OAuth flow's server-side token exchange live only in backend environment configuration.
Feature flag any significant auth flow changes (e.g., adding MFA) to allow gradual rollout and quick rollback if issues surface.
monitoring:
Monitor login success/failure rates and MFA challenge completion rates to catch both attacks (spikes in failures) and UX regressions (a broken MFA flow suddenly showing high failure rates).
Alert on anomalous patterns (many failed logins from one IP, unusual permission-denied spikes possibly indicating a frontend bug showing UI for actions users can't actually perform) in coordination with backend security monitoring.
Log (non-sensitive) auth events client-side for UX analytics (time to complete login, drop-off at MFA step) separately from security-sensitive audit logs which live on the backend.
tradeoffs:
Start with coarse-grained roles (admin/editor/viewer) and only move to fully resource-scoped, fine-grained permissions once there's a concrete product need (e.g., "editor on project X but not project Y") — building a generic fine-grained permission engine upfront, before it's needed, is a classic overengineering trap in auth systems.
Prefer httpOnly cookie-based sessions over managing JWTs in JS-accessible storage for the security benefit, even though cookies add some CSRF-mitigation complexity — this is a case where the "simpler-seeming" localStorage approach is actually the wrong trade-off given the security stakes.
Keep the frontend's permission-checking logic simple (a hook reading from already-fetched user/permission data) rather than building a complex client-side rules engine mirroring backend authorization logic — the frontend doesn't need to reimplement the backend's full authorization model, just enough to shape the UX reasonably; the backend remains the source of truth regardless.
Don't build custom SSO/OAuth flow handling from scratch — use well-established libraries/patterns for the token exchange and session handling, since auth is an area where "not reinventing the wheel" meaningfully reduces security risk.

followUpQuestions: Why is it dangerous to rely on frontend route guards as the only protection for an admin page?
How would you extend this system to support resource-scoped permissions like "editor on project X only"?
How would you handle a session that expires while the user is mid-way through filling out a long form?
What changes in your design if you need to support single sign-out across multiple products sharing one identity provider?
How would you test that your frontend permission checks actually match backend enforcement, and what happens when they drift out of sync?
spokenAnswer:
Open by stating the non-negotiable principle up front: frontend RBAC is a UX layer only, and every sensitive operation must be independently authorized server-side — this framing should anchor the entire rest of the answer.
Describe the route structure with two distinct guard types — authentication guards (are you logged in) and permission guards (are you allowed here) — and an AuthProvider context as the single source of truth for user identity and permissions, avoiding duplicated auth state across the app.
Explain the session strategy: httpOnly cookies over localStorage-stored tokens specifically to reduce XSS-based token theft risk, with transparent silent-refresh handled centrally in the HTTP client so feature code doesn't need to think about token expiry.
Cover permission granularity, explicitly recommending starting with coarse roles and only building fine-grained, resource-scoped permissions once a real product need shows up — naming this as the key place teams overengineer auth systems.
Touch error handling (careful, non-information-leaking login errors), accessibility of auth forms, and monitoring (login/MFA success rates as both security and UX signals).
Close by reiterating the trade-off: cookie-based sessions over JWT-in-localStorage despite the CSRF-mitigation overhead, and keeping frontend permission logic simple rather than mirroring the backend's full authorization model — the backend remains the actual gate no matter what the frontend shows.

title: Design a large data-table system (virtualized, filterable, sortable, server-paginated)
clarifyingQuestions: What is the expected dataset size (thousands vs. millions of rows) and typical page size the backend can efficiently serve?
Do we need client-side sort/filter for small datasets, server-side for large ones, or does it need to support both depending on context?
Are columns dynamic/configurable per user (show/hide, reorder), and how many columns are typical?
Is inline editing required, or is this purely a read/browse table?
Do we need row selection with bulk actions, and can selection persist across paginated pages?
Is this table reused across many different entity types in the product (implying it should be a generic, configurable component)?
functionalRequirements: Display large datasets with pagination (or infinite scroll) fetched from the server rather than all at once
Support sorting by column (server-driven for large datasets) and multi-column sort if needed
Support filtering (text search, faceted filters, date ranges) that updates the server query
Support column show/hide, reorder, and resize, with user preferences optionally persisted
Support row selection (single/multi) with bulk actions, including "select all matching filter" beyond just the current page
Support exporting the current filtered/sorted view (e.g., to CSV)
nonFunctionalRequirements: Must render smoothly with virtualization regardless of total dataset size — DOM node count stays bounded to roughly the visible viewport
Sort/filter/pagination state should be reflected in the URL so views are shareable/bookmarkable and survive refresh
Accessible as a data grid (proper semantics, full keyboard navigation) since dense tables are a common accessibility gap
Responsive to smaller screens (horizontal scroll or column prioritization on mobile) without breaking usability
Resilient to slow/failed server responses for any single operation (filter/sort/page change) without freezing the whole table
Reusable/configurable enough to serve multiple entity types without a rewrite per use case
routeStructure:
The table itself is typically embedded within a feature page rather than owning its own route tree, but its state is reflected in the URL's query params:
/entity-list?page=3&sort=createdAt:desc&filter[status]=active&filter[search]=foo

This means navigating back/forward, refreshing, or sharing a link preserves the exact table view the user had, and deep-linking into a specific filtered/sorted/paginated view works without any special-casing.
componentArchitecture:
A generic DataTable component takes columns (config: key, header, render function, sortable flag, width), rows (current page's data), and callbacks (onSortChange, onFilterChange, onPageChange, onSelectionChange) — it has no knowledge of what entity it's displaying, just renders the config given to it.
Internally, DataTable composes smaller pieces: a virtualized row renderer (windowing library), a TableHeader (sort indicators, resize handles), a FilterBar (rendered above, configurable per column type — text/select/date-range), a PaginationControls or infinite-scroll sentinel, and a SelectionToolbar (appears when rows are selected, showing bulk action buttons).
Each consuming feature (e.g., features/orders) defines its own column config and wires DataTable to its own service/query hook, keeping the generic table free of entity-specific logic.
Column visibility/order preferences can be lifted into a small usable hook (useTablePreferences) that optionally persists to user settings (backend) or localStorage, decoupled from the table's core rendering logic.
stateOwnership:
Server state — the actual page of rows matching the current filter/sort — is fetched via a query library, keyed by the exact filter/sort/page parameters (so switching back to a previously-viewed page/filter combination can be served from cache instantly).
Filter/sort/pagination state is the source of truth in the URL (query params), not duplicated into a separate client store — this makes the view shareable and avoids the common bug of the URL and internal state drifting out of sync.
Row selection state is ephemeral client/UI state, local to the table instance; "select all matching filter" (beyond the current page) is represented as a special selection mode (e.g., { mode: 'all', excluding: [...] }) rather than trying to materialize IDs for potentially millions of matching rows client-side.
Column visibility/order/width preferences are semi-persistent per-user UI state — small enough to store in localStorage for a quick win, or synced to the backend if cross-device consistency for these preferences matters to the product.
apiLayer:
A single, consistent list-endpoint contract (list(entityType, { page, pageSize, sort, filters })) used across all entities this table serves, returning { rows, totalCount } — this consistency is what lets one generic DataTable component work across many features.
Filter/sort/pagination changes trigger a new fetch (through the query library, which handles request deduplication and caching per unique parameter combination) rather than the table trying to filter/sort already-fetched data client-side once the dataset is server-paginated.
"Select all matching filter" bulk actions and CSV export are implemented as dedicated backend operations that accept the same filter parameters (not "fetch every row to the client and process there"), since the whole point of server-side pagination is to avoid ever pulling the full dataset into the browser.
authentication:
Row-level and field-level visibility (e.g., a user should only see rows/columns for data they're permitted to access) is enforced by the backend's list endpoint itself — filtering happens server-side as part of the query, not by fetching all rows and hiding some client-side, which would both leak data over the network and be trivially bypassable.
Bulk actions available in the SelectionToolbar are conditionally shown based on the user's permissions for UX purposes, but the backend independently validates that the authenticated user is allowed to perform the bulk action on every row it actually affects.
errorHandling:
A failed fetch for a given page/filter/sort combination shows an inline error state within the table (with a retry button) rather than a full-page crash, preserving the user's current filter/sort selections so they don't have to reconstruct their query after retrying.
Bulk actions that partially fail (e.g., "select all matching filter, delete" fails for some rows due to permission or constraint issues) report per-row or summarized failure results clearly, rather than a single ambiguous "something went wrong."
Client-side validation on filter inputs (e.g., invalid date range) is caught before firing a request; server-side validation errors on filters are surfaced inline near the relevant filter control.
caching:
The query library caches each unique (filter, sort, page) combination's result separately, so returning to a previously viewed page/filter state (e.g., via browser back button) is instant without a network round-trip, while still being fresh-checked according to a configured staleTime.
Reference data used in filter dropdowns (e.g., a list of statuses/categories) is cached longer since it changes far less often than the row data itself.
HTTP-level caching is generally not applicable to the row data itself (too dynamic/parameterized) but static table-related assets follow normal CDN caching.
performance:
Virtualization (windowing) is the core performance technique — only rows within (or near) the visible viewport are mounted in the DOM, regardless of whether the total matching dataset is 500 or 500,000 rows, since pagination bounds what's fetched and virtualization bounds what's rendered.
Debounce filter input changes (especially free-text search) before firing a new request, and cancel/ignore stale in-flight requests if the user changes filters again before the previous request resolves (a common source of "flickering" bugs where an old, slower response overwrites a newer one).
Memoize row-rendering components so a change in one row (e.g., after an inline edit) doesn't force a re-render of every visible row; keep column render functions cheap and avoid expensive computation inside them.
For very wide tables (many columns), consider column virtualization in addition to row virtualization if column count is large enough to matter.
accessibility:
Use proper table semantics (or ARIA grid pattern for interactive grids with cell-level focus) so screen readers correctly announce row/column headers and cell relationships — a plain unstructured div-based grid without ARIA roles is a common accessibility failure for custom virtualized tables.
Sortable column headers expose aria-sort and are operable via keyboard (Enter/Space to toggle sort), and filter controls are properly labeled and keyboard-accessible.
Row selection checkboxes are individually labeled (e.g., "Select row: Order #1234") rather than generic, and bulk-action availability/count is announced (aria-live) when selection changes.
Virtualized rendering must still expose correct semantics for screen readers despite only a subset of rows being in the DOM at once — this is a known hard problem with naive virtualization and often requires careful ARIA attribute management (e.g., aria-rowindex, aria-rowcount) so assistive tech understands the full dataset size even though only a window is rendered.
security:
Filter inputs are properly escaped/parameterized server-side to prevent injection when translated into backend queries (a backend concern, but the frontend should never construct raw query strings that get directly interpolated).
Exported CSV data respects the same row/field-level authorization as the on-screen table — export is just another authorized backend operation, not a way to bypass display-time filtering.
User-generated content within cells (e.g., a free-text order note column) is rendered as escaped text by default, never as raw HTML, to prevent stored XSS via table data.
testing:
Unit tests for the URL-state serialization/deserialization logic (filter/sort/page ↔ query params) since bugs here silently break shareable links and back/forward navigation.
Component tests for DataTable covering sorting, filtering, pagination, selection (including "select all matching filter" mode), and empty/loading/error states, since this component is reused broadly and bugs here are widely impactful.
Integration tests verifying that changing a filter correctly triggers a new server request with the right parameters and that stale responses are correctly discarded if superseded by a newer request.
Accessibility tests specifically targeting the virtualized grid's ARIA attributes and keyboard navigation, given how easy this is to get subtly wrong.
deployment:
The generic DataTable ships as part of the shared component library/design system (see the component library design) so improvements benefit every feature using it from a single, versioned source rather than diverging per-feature forks.
Performance regressions (e.g., virtualization scroll jank) are caught via a dedicated performance-budget check in CI (e.g., a Lighthouse or custom scroll-performance test against a large synthetic dataset) before shipping changes to this widely-used component.
Feature flag major table behavior changes (e.g., switching pagination style or filter UX) since so many features depend on this one component.
monitoring:
Track table-specific performance metrics (time-to-first-row-render, scroll frame rate, filter-to-result latency) across the products using it, since this component's performance directly affects a large surface area of the product.
Error tracking tagged by which entity/feature's table instance failed, to help pinpoint whether an issue is in the generic table or a specific feature's configuration/data.
Usage analytics on filter/sort/export usage patterns to guide prioritization of which filter types or bulk actions to invest further in.
tradeoffs:
Server-side pagination/filtering/sorting is the right default for any table that could plausibly grow large — resist the temptation to fetch "just this once, it's a small dataset" and filter/sort client-side, since that pattern tends to silently break as data grows and is genuinely harder to retrofit later than to design correctly from the start; this is one of the few places "build it right the first time" outweighs "start simple."
That said, don't over-engineer a genuinely small, bounded, rarely-growing list (e.g., a settings page listing a user's 5 API keys) with the full virtualized/server-paginated machinery — a plain client-rendered list is simpler and entirely appropriate there; match the solution to the actual data shape, not a one-size-fits-all table component used indiscriminately everywhere.
"Select all matching filter" as a selection mode (rather than materializing every matching ID client-side) is the right approach even though it's slightly more complex to implement, because the naive approach breaks down completely at scale and creates a false sense of "it works" that fails exactly when the dataset gets large enough to matter.
Building a single generic, configurable DataTable used everywhere is worth the upfront design investment once there are three or more distinct tables in the product — before that, a bespoke table per feature may genuinely be simpler and premature abstraction into a "one table to rule them all" component can slow early development without enough reuse to justify it yet.
